The spread of e-commerce platforms, streaming services and social media networks has fundamentally changed the way consumers discover and choose products, content and information. In the centre of this change is recommendation algorithm—a computational mechanism to predict user preferences and filter mass of choices in a personalised way into satisfactory options. The evolution of algorithms towards those based on collaborative filtering, content-based filtering and even deep learning combined with their potential influence on consumer decision-making have sparked significant academic interest across a number of fields including marketing, information systems, psychology and computer science.

Initial studies in this area mostly concentrated on the technical effectiveness of recommender systems, focusing on accuracy scores and performance at an algorithmic level. But as these systems have become more and more a part of day to day consumer experiences, researchers started examining the potential behavioral and psychological ramifications. With only a few exceptions, most appear pretty good (e.g. we observe the question of whether recommendation algorithms actually serve to benefit consumers by lowering search costs and information overload or instead limit choice architecture in ways that undermine autonomy, induce similar preferences, and make filter bubbles). At the same time, studies have investigated the interplay of algorithmic recommendations with trust, perceived personalization and serendipity in influencing purchase intentions as well as attitudinal satisfaction.

Nonetheless, although the literature on CA systems is growing, major controversial discussions are ongoing regarding how their net effects influence quality and diversity of consumer choice as well as long-term skills to make sound decisions. We will explore the benefits and detriments of recommendation. Some scholars argue that recommendation algorithms actually empower consumers by pushing relevant options to them they might not come across, while others warn that dependency on algorithmic curation threatens critical thinking around consumption so we move into echophelia where we all consume the same rubbish as each other. Moreover, transparency, manipulation and algorithmic bias have made it hard to grasp what these systems do with consumer agency.

This review integrates previous research on the effects of recommendation algorithms on consumer choice, applying essential theories, evidence from empirical studies, and approaches to methodology. This purportedly serves to clarify the existing areas of agreement and disagreement, discover the missing knowledge in relation to this emergent but burgeoning area of consumer behavior, and suggest new avenues for future research into this increasingly important area of consumer behavior.

**Document Your Impact**
They are anecdotal at best, the opposite of what you want for an investment pitch. Quantify your contributions clearly. You want to make a note of moments when the leadership, mentorship provided and how you solved important problems. This isn't bragging—it's evidence.

**Prepare a Clear Narrative**
Talk about what your did outside of the scope of you role. Describe how the project allowed you to take on more responsibility and grow your skill set. Link your growth to the demands of the next level. Demonstrate that you were already operating on a higher frequency

Schedule a focused meeting with your boss—don't call them on the fly. **During the Conversation**
Start with gratitude for the chances you have gotten in your life. Present your accomplishments without defensiveness. For example: “I led cross-functional coordination on successfully shipping the project on-time, and under-budget. Just ask barring no questions, "Considering what I have accomplished so far, I think I am ready to move up into [position]. What are your thoughts?"

**Listen to Feedback**
Your manager can say yes, lay out next steps for you, or chart the gaps. If they're hesitant, inquire about what they need: "What can I do to help you get there? Make notes and an actionable plan.

**Follow Up**
Make an appointment for a 90-day check-in if it is no. Keep providing value and acting on the feedback received. If yes, then put details in writing.

Yes, buying your first telescope can be a confusing business but it shouldn't do. Here are 10 easy strategies you can use to choose one that you will actually want to use.

1. **Skip the “highest magnification” hype. Big magnification numbers look great on paper but image quality is far more important. Every time, a wide-view stable trumpils the blurry close-up.

2. **Look at aperture first. ** Aperture - Diameter of the telescope main lens or mirror. More aperture gathers more light, making Moon and planets and faint objects easier to see.

3. **Start with a simple mount. Typically, a mount is an alt-azimuth mount that moves up/down and left/right, which is probably the simplest to use. Setup can be painful with mount that are overly complicated.

4. **Consider a tabletop Dobsonian. ** These small reflector telescopes are typically very inexpensive, stable and easy to aim. They are the ideal option for children and adults alike.

5. **Avoid department-store telescopes. ** Bicycle retailer-general-grade scopes with weak tripods and bling-bling decorative packaging can be an enormous bummer. A smaller, well-built scope is the better choice from any reputable astronomy dealer.

6. **Think about portability. The best telescope is the one that you will use. If it is too heavy or cumbersome to get outdoors — best-case scenario; it gathers dust in a closet.

7. **Don’t forget binoculars. 8x42 or 10x50 binoculars are quite adequate and would be an excellent first step. They are intuitive to use and pretty darn fun for astronomy.

8. **Check what accessories are included. Essentials are two eyepieces, a finder scope and mount strong enough to hold the telescope publicly. You may not want an accessory bundle right at the start.

9. **Use astronomy apps. ** Apps like Stellarium or SkySafari can connect to stars, planets and constellations. It makes your first nights outside a whole lot less daunting.

10. **Set realistic expectations. Planets will not be as cohesive as NASA pictures, but looking up at the rings of Saturn or with your own eyes moons orbiting around Jupiter is still impressive.

Keep it simple, keep it enjoyable, take a few evenings to get familiar with the sky. Your first telescope does not have to be a make-or-break device; it just needs to be capable of getting you outside and looking up!

Hybrid learning is not the death of the university lecture but its inevitable transformation. Rent stabilization, which works against housing affordability crises and in favor of eviction protections for some tenants, is a particularly complicated social and economic trade-off in urban policy. The overall justification for these measures is based on the premise that housing markets by themselves will not always produce a sufficient supply of affordable housingâ€”especially for low-income householdsâ€”and that the presence of unregulated housing markets may result in excessively high and exploitive rents and reduced security. But rent stabilization is rarely implemented lightly, and it often sparks rigorous debate among policymakers, economists, and housing advocates about its effectiveness in practice versus theory. This literature review seeks to investigate the complex trade-offs associated with rent stabilization programs, including the admittedly favorable and adverse effects.

Extensive evidence supports rent stabilization as an essential tenant protection policy that can prevent speculative values from being reflected in rents and thereby keep tenants in their homes, stabilizing neighborhoods and communities by helping ensure they are not involuntarily displaced. Supporters claim that these measures make housing more affordable, especially in areas where gentrification is occurring rapidly, and so create a fairer distribution of housing. On the other hand, a major criticism points out that rent controls distort market signals, reduce incentives to build new or take care of existing housing stock, and may invoke an ironical trend in the long term: shortage raising pressure on prices and state of disrepair falling. This paper seeks to elaborate on these conflicting views by bringing together empirical findings related to the effect of rent stabilization on rents, housing supply, property values, landlord responses and tenant welfare. We conduct a systematic review of the literature to yield a high-level overview with a differences-in-differences approach, as well as an ongoing area of agreement and contention in the academic and policy world about rent stabilization's economic and social tradeoffs.

## The Limitation of Regulating Facial Recognition

Facial recognition technology does raise some real privacy issues but there is a danger in imposing too many regulations for fear of harming innovation and implementing a framework that will be ineffectual.

Advocates of draconian regulation point to facial recognition as a tool for mass surveillance that jeopardizes civil liberties. But this line of reasoning ignores an important reality: only limited regulation can prevent motivated actors from creating or deploying such technology. But authoritarian regimes and criminals will find a way to get their hands on these tools regardless of the impropriety. If we regulate facial recognition so strictly in democracies, we are effectively handing over the technology to less ethical players.

Furthermore, extremely restrictive regulations do not facilitate the considerable benefits of facial recognition. This technology is used by law enforcement agencies for recognizing suspects in serious crimes, tracking down abducted children and fighting against human trafficking. It is used by banks to prevent fraud and for secure authentication. Medical researchers use it to study genetic disorders. These blanket restrictions also remove otherwise responsible uses of the technology, along with irresponsible ones.

The main issue with regulation is that it is not adaptable for change. Technology evolves quickly, often faster than lawmaking. Instead of creating inflexible rules that will get outlived, let us concentrate on standards for accuracy, requirements for transparency and mechanisms of accountability which are upgradable with technological progress? Companies should be compelled to announce that they are using facial recognition, individuals ought to have recourse against facial recognition when it fails or is misused â€” but not all of those effects means banning the technology in and of itself.

Additionally, the regulations on facial recognition vary significantly by jurisdiction, resulting in compliance headaches with little imposed privacy benefit. An image posted to an American social media company is still open up for non-restricted worldwide facial recognition analysis.

Policymakers should replace unattainable bans with use-case clarity and audit capabilities to promote responsible deployment. The optimal regulation is when regulations work as minimum standards but with the room for innovation. With facial recognition, frameworks less strict will look out for privacy better than regulation that pushes development underground or overseas.

Unlimited vacation policies, sometimes calledality “discretionary time off” or “flexible leave,” have become a popular perk among organizations attempting to attract and retain talent. Unlike traditional paid time off, which allocates a blocked number of vacation days and may require workers to accrue their leave over the length of employment, unlimited vacation permits employees to take time away from work as needed provided they have management and/or the business requirement (which other firm must history assures will be minimal). Advocates say such policies communicate deeply held trust in employees, an effort to promote work–life balance for their workers, and the necessity of aligning employee benefits with a time when many firms are demanding flexibility and autonomy from white-collar professionals. These perceived advantages may make unlimited vacation a particularly attractive retention tool, especially within knowledge-work industries and to employees who value control over when and how they work, in competitive labor markets.

But on the other hand unlimited vacation does not default to a direct correlation with employee retention. Flexible leave can alleviate administrative burdens and meet employees' personal, family, and health needs, potentially enhancing employee satisfaction but unlimited policies also lead an ambiguity. In a high-performance or understaffed environment, employees may have little idea as to how much time off from work is socially acceptable. The literature on norms and in workplace behaviour indicates that employees face common sense anxiety when given vague expectations and end up either under- or over-utilising it, particularly out of concerns that they will come off as less committed than their peers if they take the leave they might otherwise be entitled to. As a result, unlimited vacation may behave quite differently, depending on organizational culture, the behavior of leaders or managers thereof, workload, psychological safety and how much leaders actually model time away from work.

The retention literature thus suggests that compensation and benefits are seldom a primary driver of turnover. Job satisfaction, perceived organizational support, fairness, burnout, career opportunities and relationships with supervisors influence employees’ decisions to stay with an employer. As such, unlimited vacation may be best as one piece of a larger retention strategy instead of an isolated perk. Providing flexible leave alongside adequate staffing, clear usage guidelines, supportive leadership and equitable access by role may reinforce employee perception of how much the organization values their well-being. Conservation ecology as a passion began with noticing the fragility and interdependence of systems before I ever set foot in a classroom. As I watched a local wetland near my home shrink every year to development, I realised that the loss of such ecosystems is rarely just the loss of a single species or splitter — it is the collapse of multitudes up hold-ing life well beyond what we can see. This acknowledgment gave rise to an intense fascination with the forces that bind ecosystems together, and those anthropogenic pressures that threaten fraying.

This interest eventually developed into a dedicated interest in understanding biodiversity loss, habitat fragmentation and the wider impacts of climate change. You work with local diminishing environmental groups, track species population through citizen science projects and engage with the literature in restoration ecology and sustainable land management. Although this experience has broadened my worldview, it more prominently reaffirmed what I have always believed – conservation is not a matter of protecting nature for its own good, but instead the preservation of ecological infrastructure on which human societies rely.

The most attractive aspect of conservation ecology to me is the combination between solid science and practical application. I am excited to learn how we can use quantitative approaches, fieldwork, and ecological theory to address urgent environmental problems in addition to knowledge of the political and community factors that mediate whether conservation programs succeed or fail in practice. This is the effort I want to contribute to, equipped with science (and other) skills and an honest interest in how we live in relationship with nature – conservation ecology is my next first step that will allow me to make authentic contributions.

Preparing for system-design interviews is not simply a rote memorization of architectures from books and papers. Try to create a process that allows you to translate vague requirements into designs that are actionable and scalable.

First, read the basics: Scalability, Availability, Consistency, Latency. Partitioning. Replication. Caching. Load Balancing. Queues :bulb: Databases and Failure recovery Learn the trade-offs and do not memorize definitions. Enjoy being able to explain when you might want SQL vs NoSQL, synchronous vs asynchronous communication, strong vs eventual consistency.

Practice class design egurl shortener, messaging system (like WhatsApp), social feed, file storage, ride-sharing platform, and video service. For each of the problems, follow this same framework:

1. Clarify requirements. What are the characteristics of the entities you would like to model?Who will use these models, how will they be used, and what user traffic metrics do you expect?What is the size of data expected to be loaded in this model, what latency can it tolerate and how often does this change?
2. Estimate capacity. Estimate request per sec, storage, bandwidth and growth with ballpark figures State assumptions clearly.
3. Specification of the API and data model Make them simple and relevant to the dominant use cases.
4. Draw the high-level architecture. Story Where The Client interacts with the service interacts with database / cache / queue / external system
5. Explore bottlenecks and failures. Talk replication, sharding, retries, timeouts, backpressure, monitoring and disaster recovery
6. Revisit trade-offs. Describe why the choices that you made satisfy the criteria â€” what would you alter in a bigger deployment?

Practice out loud â€” with a timer. Interviewers want to assess critical communication and decision-making on par with pure tech knowledge. Do not start by explaining how you would implement it, before having figured out what the overall design should look like and do not assume that there is one solution that applies everywhere.

Research how real systems work â€” study the architecture of well-known systems and review engineering case studies. Before the interview, prepare a short framework structuring your response, ensure good practice in estimations and get comfortable with asking clarifying questions. In the interview, work together, own your uncertainty and adapt your design to new constraints.

10 Tips for Moving a Rescue Cat into a New Apartment

Feeding a cat with Oh, goodness is one of the absolute epitomes of everything. However, moving from a shelter to your nice warm apartment can be quite the change for your new friend. To assist them in settling, the following are 10 quick ideas to ensure a smooth transition.

**1. Start with a "safe zone"**
Why not give them full run of the place from second one. Put them in a very small quiet room (like a bathroom or bedroom) with food, water, and litter.

**2. Keep it quiet**
Don't throw a housewarming party yet. Refrain from loud noises for a few days so that you do not startle your cat with sudden noise.

**3. Provide hiding spots**
Cats love to hide when they are uncertain. Leave their carrier open, or create a cardboard box with a warm blanket in it.

**4. Keep the litter box accessible**
Keep the litter box in a calm, low-traffic area. Multi-story loft? You may need one on each level when you first get started.

**5. Cat-proof your balcony**
Yes, balconies at the apartments but safety before all! If you're thinking about letting your kitty out on your balcony, be sure to catproof it first by putting netting over the top!

**6. Stick to a routine**
Feed them at the same time each day Having simple predictability gives rescue cats a sense of security.

**7. Use pheromones**
Introduce a synthetic pheromone diffuser (for example, Feliway) in their safe room It acts like magic and is made with natural calming scents.

**8. Block tight spaces**
Seal gap behind washing machine or under heavy furniture where they may get trapped.

**9. Go vertical**
Space is limited when it comes to apartments--go high! A tall cat tree or a window perch will provide them with a good lookout spot to view the outside.

**10. Let them set the pace**
Others take weeks, while some cats adjust in hours. Let cuddles always come to you -never force them.

Do the same and soon enough they will be the boss!

Print-on-demand (POD) has radically changed the economics of self-publishing, removing one critically important barrier that imposed little on the success chances of independent authors: initial capital. Prior to POD (print on demand), self-publishing meant having an offset print run of hundreds or even thousands of copies commissioned, often costing authors thousands of dollars before selling a one. That created considerable financial risk, compelled authors to warehouse stock, and often left many with a garage shelf full of bookstore returns.

POD technology turned this model on its head, since books can now be printed one at a time, by order from those who really want one. This change in turn turned publishing from an inventory business to a "just-in-time" service, from a highly fixed-cost structure to one based on low-risk variable costs. It means that authors do not have to guess which books will sell ahead of time and pay for printing; instead, their book is only printed after a sale occurs and the cost is deducted from the revenue.

This has opened the doors of publishing to many new writers with little resources, allowing them to enter books into market. It has also changed profit calculations: printing per unit is more expensive than traditional offset print, shaving margins on each copy but counterbalanced by the lack of upfront investment and una=sold inventory. Moreover, POD can be fully integrated with e-commerce and thus provides global distribution without physical storage.

This big change has resulted in a long-tail effect, with not just an increase of self-published titles but a revolutionizing shift which went through the equation "can I afford to publish this book?" into "will somebody buy it" â€“ and when you combine that financial calculus then the stakes behind creative and entrepreneurial risk-taking in publishing are inherently lowered.

With these suburban regions quickly growing, local governments are coming under heavy pressure to uplift public transit outside original cities. Recent housing developments, traffic congestion and longer travel times have. increased pressure for dependable bus and rail service in communities previously planned for automobiles exclusively.

Increased investment is also key to transit advocates if they want to maintain the boom in sustainable growth. Home to few public transportation options can leave residents without cars stranded in places like quickly expanding suburbs— seniors, students and lower-paid employees who do not have the means to afford a car are cut off from jobs, schools and health care. Better service alsocuts traffic stress and undergirds denser development at stations and along high-frequency bus corridors.

Suburban transit agencies get by on a blend of local taxes, state grants and federal help—revenues that can vary with economic conditions. While major cities often have established transit systems and revenue sources to fund growth, many suburban communities are literally building networks and facilities from the ground up.

Others local officials have floated boosts to sales tax hikes, special assessment districts and public-private partnerships for financing expansion. While some others are pursuing federal infrastructure grants to buy electric buses, upgrade stops or extend rail lines. The train-train debate will only sharpen as suburbs grow. The choices in the immediate term will help to decide whether expansion leads to fresh car-centric places — or public transport-friendly communities.

The explosion of e-commerce, streaming, and social media creates a hyper-competitive marketplace where consumers make countless decisions about content and products. Prior research focuses on the shortcomings and improvements of recommendation systems. More recently, psychologists and social scientists have expanded the scope to evaluate recommendation systems based on their impact on consumer choice, especially in relation to welfare and ethics. The research explores if recommendation systems enhance consumer welfare, or if they constrain consumer choice by recommending only items within a filter bubble, thereby reducing the range of choices available to the consumer. Further, researchers have studied consumersâ€™ perception of recommendations in conjunction with their intent to purchase.

While more studies are being done, there is still a great deal of controversy concerning the body of work in this area. There are some experts in this field who believe that recommendation systems give consumers more choices. Others believe that if recommendation systems are relied upon too much, consumers will become dependent upon the systems and will stop making their own choices. It is possible that in the future, recommendation systems will be widely used. If this happens, the consequences, both good and bad, will affect consumers globally.

In this paper, the effects of recommendation systems on consumer choices will be reviewed. This review will analyze and outline various theories concerning recommendation systems and consumer choices. Additional aspects of this review will include the methods and data collected in various recommendation systems studies. This paper hopes to achieve an understanding of the major viewpoints and minor viewpoints pertaining to recommendation systems. It is the goal of this review to achieve a more complete knowledge of this area and to suggest and prioritize areas for further research in this field.

# 10 Tips for Choosing a Beginner Telescope

Buying your first telescope can be an overwhelming experience. These 10 guidelines will help you with your purchase and get you enjoying your telescope faster.
1. Ignore the false marketing of high magnification.
The quality of the image is much more important than the power of the telescope. A clear image of the moon is much better than a blurry close-up image.
2. Look at the aperture.
The bigger the aperture is, the more light the telescope can collect. This can help bring out details on fainter objects.
3. Look for a simple mount.
For beginners, a simple alt-azimuth mount will work best. More complex mounts will only serve to frustrate the user.
4. Consider a Dobsonian.
Dobsonian telescopes are easy to use and move in and out of position easily. 
5. Avoid cheap telescopes.
Department stores usually carry low quality telescopes that do not give a good first time experience to Astronomy.
6. Consider how easy it is to transport.
A large and heavy telescope is of no use if it is never taken out.
7. Consider using binoculars.
A good pair of binoculars can be a great starting point for astronomical observations.
8. Saturn is rising!
Saturn is a great first object to view with a new telescope.
9. Use good judgement for accessories.
Not all accessories are created equal. Purchasing good quality accessories can improve your first telescope buying experience.
10. Donâ€™t forget to look at reviews.
For first time buyers, reviews can help explain features and give buying tips.

8. Some basics to consider when buying your first telescope include whether it includes two eyepieces, a finder scope, and a sturdy mount. The first couple of months or a year probably won't depend too much on extra accessories.

9. astronomy apps are a great, initial resource. Some great options include Stellarium and SkySafari. These types of programs are great aids while learning. 

10. One thing to set expectations for, is planetary imagery. Telescopes don't magnify images to the extent most people assume. However, seeing moons of Jupiter and rings of Saturn are awesome sights. 

Lastly, remember that this should be fun! The goal should not be to purchase the highest end scope. Hopefully this assists in your purchasing decision.

Self check out solutions change the way stores interact with their customers. Traditionally, the check out counter was a place where customers interacted with store employees and therefore interacted with the store brand. Automating check out counters means stores no longer employ staff to interact with customers. With automation, the store changes customers from people being “served” to people “doing the serving.”

This situation creates a situation where customers feel more alienated than ever before. For some customers this situation is actually preferable to interacting with other humans. Customers can check out on their own and leave without speaking to an employee. Self check out gives customers a way to check out without social interaction.

While this situation may seem preferable to some customers, this situation creates a very hostile environment. Employees of the store, known as “monitor(s)” in self check out lingo, view self check out customers as potential thieves. Customers can make the store employee think they are a thief by making a trivial error while using the self check out machine.

In an attempt to make the check out process as cheap as possible, some stores have completely automated the check out process. This situation has devastating effects on the customer and staff members of the store. The store becomes a location to transact goods rather than a part of the community. In the end, self check out makes stores, and other similar retail establishments, indistinguishable from a large warehouse.

# Independent Newsletter Writers

The last few years have shown us that newsletter writers are able to blend analysis, opinion, and reporting in a way that captures the attention of a discerning audience. They have learned to identify and fill the voids in specific areas of the news and commentary spectrum. 

Writing and delivering news is no longer the domain of large media houses. Newsletters have given writers a means to distribute commentary and analysis outside the control of traditional gatekeepers. Newsletters have been very effective in building an audience interested in a particular kind of journalism. 

Newsletter writers have a direct relationship with their audience. This allows them to build a following based on trust, and helps them bridge the gap that has developed as a result of faceless, large and often unaccountable media outlets. 

 newsletter writers have plenty of opportunities to earn a living and be successful in writing without relying on traditional and often unsupportive gatekeeping structures. Substack and other similar sites have allowed writers to charge for their newsletters and liberated them from the structuring and binding confines of conventional journalism.

They've found success for a couple of reasons. For one, newsletter writers are able to dive deep and develop knowledge and passion for specific topics. Compared to other journalists, newsletter writers have a more consistent voice and perspective, so readers donâ€™t have to speculate on the authorâ€™s personal views and biases.

Of course, writers do have their limitations. With no traditional gatekeeping, misinformation has flourished. There are hundreds of newsletters covering the same topics, so itâ€™s often difficult to decipher who is really in charge and how accountable writers and newsletters really are.

Thereâ€™s also been a blurring of lines in the journalism industry. Established journalists are able to leverage their experience to develop success in the newsletter industry, often doing both at the same time. These dueling industries seem to support and reinforce one other.

Because of the saturation of audiences and the fact that traditional media often feels distant and unengaging, newsletter writers are able to produce and disseminate quality, trustworthy journalism in the format of their choosing. Informed and passionate writing is often exactly what people want to read. It fulfills a niche between social media and traditional media.

Lecturing has withstood the test of time and, when reformed, will continue to be a valuable method of shaping and conveying bodies of knowledge.

Rent stabilization is an area of housing policy that creates a number of social and economic trade-offs. On the one hand, unfair and sudden changes to the housing market can put the most vulnerable members of the population at risk by leaving them homeless. In areas with high housing costs, there is an acute risk of exploitation by landlords who charge what the market can bear. Ultimately, tenants can lose access to adequate and stable housing. Because of these issues, rent regulation was created to make sure that tenants, especially the most vulnerable, do not lose housing protection. While rent stabilization creates a number of social benefits, the policy has economic costs. The main aim of this literature review is to outline the costs of rent stabilization, as well as to identify the benefits of the policy.

Many studies support rent regulation as a key element of stabilizing the housing market and protecting tenants. It especially helps in reducing unnecessary moves. Rent increases lead to the forced move of tenants, and rent regulated apartments have lower rates of moves. Rent regulated apartments also make affordability improvements in areas that experience gentrification. Rent regulations improve the overall equity in housing. However, some studies point out that, in the long term, rent regulations negatively impact housing. This is because the regulations reduce the incentive for landlords to improve or repair their housing. The purpose of this study is to analyze the various studies that evaluated the impact of rent regulations and drew conclusions regarding the price of rentals, the quality of housing, the behaviors of landlords, and the welfare of tenants. This study will use the conclusions drawn from the literature to identify the most sensible and productive policy changes regarding rent regulations.

Training to complete your first 100-mile century ride is a gradual process that requires consistency and dedication. You will strengthen your cardiovascular system and train your muscles to endure the rigors of a century ride with the required nutritional and hydration habits over the course of 20 weeks.

 1-4 Weeks: Establishing your Base

Prepare to train a minimum of 3-4 days a week. During this period concentrate on developing the habit of regular training and improving your cardiovascular endurance. Achieve this by rising to a 45-60 minute training duration by the end of the period. The key to each of these rides is pace not effort; concentrate on maintaining a pace at which you could hold a conversation. The longer and more strenuous training of the week is a training achievement goal of 25 miles which will increase to 30 miles by week 4. 

5-8 Weeks: Progressing your Training

Practice the use of climbing and/or rising to a higher cadence to improve leg strength and endurance for 1 hour each week. Achieve this by adding hill repeats or intervals to your training. The longer and more strenuous training goal of the week is a 45 mile ride which will increase to a 60 mile ride by the end of this period. During longer training rides practice fueling by consuming a minimum of 30-60 grams of carbohydrates and a fluid replacement electrolyte beverage.

**Weeks 9-12: Peaking Weeks**

These weeks represent the training for the event by showing the weekly volume required. You will do a slight increase in your weekday training and your weekends will include your long rides. Aim for 70 mile rides in week 9 and increase to a week 12 long ride of 80-85 miles. If you can do an 85 mile training ride then you should be able to do a century with no problem.

**Weeks 13-16: Events and Recovery**

Continue to do training rides, but progressively do fewer and shorter rides. Aim for a week 14 training ride of 50 miles and a week 15 ride of 30 miles. To be fully prepared and ready to go for the event do two short rides in week 16. During the rides you should focus on taking care of your body by hydrating and get some rest.

Extreme weather conditions alter people’s attitudes toward homeownership. The last several hurricanes and wildfires have shown that homeownership brings significant risks. People purchase homes to provide a sense of security and independence; however, the value of that investment is dramatically reduced if the home is located in a high-risk flood or wildfire area. Home values are reduced if key infrastructure (schools, hospitals, and roads) are located outside the homeowner’s insurance limits.

Purchasing a home creates new risks, and people are increasingly focused on the location of home services, the type of construction, the energy efficiency of a home, and the resilience of home utilities. Meanwhile, the square footage of a school, and the school’s location, are declining in importance. Adaptation to changing weather conditions has benefitted some homeowners at the expense of others. People with the financial means can move to a safer area or retrofit their homes, while people with low to moderate incomes are often forced to remain in high risk areas and suffer increasing costs of insurance.

Extreme weather shows that homeownership is a communal accomplishment. Safety and security depend on many communal choices from zoning to public services and preparation to ease the burden on communities most threatened by extreme events. Some places may determine that protecting the safety and security of communities may include a shift to temporary, cooperative, or publicly owned housing.

 Extreme weather events change the nature of homeownership. Homeownership may be more about safety and security from increasingly severe, extreme weather events and less about owning a permanent refuge. Home ownership may require balancing a number of values including protection of the environment and adaptation to climate change.

CHICAGO – Tyler Chen, now 10, used to love the game of baseball. However, after two years of playing on a competitive travel team that practices three times and plays tournaments on the weekends, he decided to take a break from organized sports.

“The practice and travel made him really tired. He lost his love for the game,” said his mother Sarah Chen. 

Studies have shown Tyler’s case to be representative of a larger trend of childhood burnout. Early sports specialization is on the rise among children. 

As young as seven years old, children are being pressured by parents to specialize in a sport, train intensely, and compete all year long. Experts say this trend has negative consequences and does more harm than good.

"Overuse injuries like Tommy John surgeries for kids in middle school have begun to increase dramatically," Dr. Murray said. "Also increasing is the anxiety and depression children and adolescents suffer when they sustain an injury. Many children and adolescents have their self-worth tied to their sporting ability and performance. For those children, suffering an injury can be perceived as an identity crisis."

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has stated that children and adolescents should avoid sport specialization until at least the completion of adolescent growth and development (i.e. approximately 15-16 years of age). The AAP stated that sport sampling is appropriate for children and adolescents, and can delay sport burnout, and provide cross-training benefits to the individual.

Seventy percent of children and adolescents stop participating in organized sports by the time they turn 13 years of age.

One example of the negative impact of youth sport specialization is Tyler. Tyler's parents provided him with the opportunity to engage in unstructured (i.e. free play) sports activities to provide him with a break from competitive sports.

While there are justifiable concerns about the effect of facial recognition technology on personal privacy, it is possible to regulate the technology in a way that allays privacy concerns and, at the same time, encourages and facilitates the continued development of the technology.

Because regulation has little effect on the development and deployment of this technology by nation-states and other organized, malicious groups, regulation aimed at safeguarding the civil liberties of a population by prohibiting the use of facial recognition technology will ultimately be ineffective. Civil liberties will be undermined by unscrupulous malicious actors and the technology will continue to advance.

It is also important to recognize the positive impacts of facial recognition technology. This technology is used to assist law enforcement in solving and preventing crimes and helping to locate and protect children and other vulnerable groups. This technology promotes business and facilitates the practice of medicine.

If the focus is on developing the positive impacts of the technology, while encouraging consideration of thenegative impacts, it may be possible to establish a regulatory framework that protects the civil liberties of a population and maintains the rule of law.

The main problem with any regulation is that it is nearly impossible to create regulations that adapt to and accommodate the rapidly changing technological environment. Instead of regulating the use of facial recognition by imposing bans and restrictions on its use, we should set performance standards and/or monitoring requirements that are technology-neutral and adaptable. In addition, a person should have the right to sue and/or seek other legal remedies for any harm caused by the use of facial recognition. Finally, companies should be required to disclose the use of facial recognition by employees or agents of the company.

There are relatively few restrictions on the use of facial recognition in the U.S., and the regulations that do exist vary from state to state. However, out of country restrictions should be of more concern. A photo posted on a U.S. based social network instantly loses any U.S. privacy protections and becomes available for international, unrestricted, facial recognition.

Most regulations work best when they create a minimum standard and leave the rest to the marketplace. Similarly, the best regulatory approach to facial recognition would allow for a flexible standard and encourage technological development. However, the current trend of facial recognition regulation creates an undue burden on legitimate development and encourages it to occur outside of the U.S.

Unlimited vacation policies provide employees with the ability to take as much time off as they desire. Companies have started implementing these policies in order to recruit and retain employees. With traditional vacation policies, employees are given a limited number of vacation days and often times are forced to take a personal day in order to take time off if they have not reached their annual limit. Aside from signaling management’s trust, an unlimited vacation policy gives employees the ability to take time off when they see fit. This can help employees integrate their personal and work lives. Many employees, especially knowledge workers, can control their own schedules and decide when and where they work.

Although employee satisfaction with an unlimited policy is high, this does not always guarantee retention. Flexible vacation policies often reduce employee dissatisfaction because of the lack of vacation day administration. Often times, employees feel anxious because of the ambiguity associated with unlimited policies. Employees often times take less time off than they feel entitled to because they fear appearing less committed than their coworkers. In order to fully understand why an unlimited vacation policy works the way it does, many factors including management style, workplace culture, and psychological safety, must be taken into account.

More research has shown that benefits and wages, by themselves, generally do not lead to voluntary turnover. Employees decide to stay or leave based on a combination of factors, including the availability of opportunities outside the organization, supervisory relationships, the employee’s level of burnout, the organization’s support and fairness, and the employee’s level of job satisfaction. Consequently, a better retention strategy might incorporate unlimited vacation time along with other changes. If combined with adequate staffing levels, unlimited vacation time, along with other types of leave, might help retain employees and show the organization’s support for employee well-being. Based on the literature available, this review explores the negative and positive consequences of unlimited vacation time on employee well-being, voluntary turnover, and workplace norms and culture.

Prior to POD, the major financial barrier to entry in the book publishing market was the upfront cost of book production. This cost was measured in the thousands of dollars and typically required authors to raise capital to fund book print runs in the hundreds or thousands of copies. This cost placed the potential benefit of book sales (recovery of the investment and a profit) against the risk of an unstable and uncertain marketplace (book inventory). Often, authors wound up with an unmanageable book inventory.

POD changed this model. Now authors had the ability to publish books without assuming the financial risk of predicting and satisfying potential demand. POD revolved around a demand-based model in which a book was printed once a customer placed an order. Author risk became aligned with financial risk, and the author no longer had to cover the cost of book production. Instead, the book was printed when a customer placed an order and the author's financial risk was reduced to the cost of stocking and managing the inventory of the book.

Some authors believed POD would democratize the book publishing industry. This was due to the fact that POD reduced the financial barriers to book production and removed the risk of book inventory. Now authors could recover the cost of a book production run once potential demand for a book was satisfied.

The expansion of suburbia creates a burgeoning need for public transit options outside central city locations. More housing developments lead to more commuters using already congested roads and highways. Suburbs that were planned to be dependent on the automobile for transportation need bus and rail options to provide commuters with an alternative to driving.

 It is acknowledged by all interested parties that more funding needs to be directed towards improving suburban transit systems. Too often, the suburban transit systems that are in place leave people without access to transportation to jobs and other essential services. 

The fact that more people are using a transit system increases the need to build and improve the system, particularly if a community wants to decrease the number of automobiles on the road and foster more people living in the community and using the transit system. Improving public transit is a double edged sword; it encourages dense, urban living and reduces suburban sprawl. 

Funding remains the final barrier to improving public transit systems. Unlike major cities, many suburban areas are forced to create their public transit systems from the ground up, with very little (if any) dedicated funding.

To pay for improvements, local governments are considering sales tax increases, creating special assessment districts, and/or entering into public private partnerships. Other governments are applying for Federal grants to enhance public transportation.

Long-term improvements to public transit are justified by the expectation that new users will foster a positive economic impact and lead to increased property values and greater business development.

Improvements to public transit systems are costly, and some question if the systems will pay for themselves. From a fiscal impact perspective, some are critical of public transit systems because they do not alleviate traffic in low-density areas and may lead to increased taxes. 

Improving public transit to and from the suburbs is difficult and requires more effort than starting a new transit route. Better integration with other public transit systems is crucial. Well planned and designed land use and zoning policies can help locate employment and residential districts near public transit to improve usage.

The rise of online shopping, streaming services as well as social media has changed the way consumers find and choose products, content, and information. At the core of this process lies the recommendation algorithm, which is a system that predicts user preferences and filters the many possible options that may have been available. As these algorithms got more and more advanced due to collaborative filtering as well as content filtering techniques, interest in the influence recommendation algorithms exert on consumers increased among scholars across a number of different areas.

Initially, this research was more focused on the performance of recommendation systems in terms of effectiveness and accuracy, but once these systems were introduced into everyday practice, the research shifted to behavioral and psychological implications of recommendation systems. The questions were raised whether recommendation algorithms are actually increasing consumer welfare in terms of access to the information by offering consumers a wide selection of options available or if they are actually limiting choice architectures resulting in putting consumers in a narrow box in terms of the decision-making. Moreover, researchers looked at algorithmic recommendations in interaction with trust, perceived personalization as well as serendipity in terms of purchase intentions and product satisfaction.

Nonetheless, the scholarship is not over as a number of controversies exist in terms of the net effect of recommendation systems on consumer choice behavior as well as consumption diversity. Some scholars believe that recommendation algorithms enhance the decision-making process while others warn that they may lead to the loss of independent judgment and, therefore, homogeneity in terms of consumption. Furthermore, ethical and moral considerations regarding the recommendation systems have appeared in research as well.

The article proposes a review of recent studies that investigate the effects of recommendation algorithms on consumer choice and consumption process. approaches. In doing so, it aims to clarify areas of consensus and contention, identify gaps in current knowledge, and propose directions for future research into this increasingly consequential domain of consumer behavior.

# How to Seek a Promotion Following the Successful Completion of a Major Project

**Choose the Right Time**
After the launch of the project, wait for 2-4 weeks before organizing a meeting. This waiting time enables to reach some results and provides the stakeholders with the required distance to analyze the project’s influence impartially. Do not ask for a meeting right away; otherwise you will give people an impression of opportunism instead of strategic thinking.

**Gather Information About Your Achievements**
Collect all data about the key indicators of your work: profits earned, expenses saved, number of users and the increased efficiency of the process. Be specific about your contributions to the work. Note the leadership positions you held and the hard cases you had to deal with. This is not boasting but a proof of your success.

**Prepare Your Speech in Advance**
Outline what you have done apart from your job duties and describe how this particular project has broadened your functions and responsibilities. Connect your experience with what is demanded from people of a higher level. 

**Plan the Meeting Appropriately**
Do not surprise your supervisor; send him/her a request for a meeting. Write in the direct manner saying that you wish to speak about your career advancement and your achievements at work.

**During the Meeting**
Announce your gratitude and express your appreciation of what you have accomplished so far. Mention your accomplishments and do not feel defensive. Be specific and mention that the project was finished on time and did not exceed the budget. Ask about the possibility of being promoted.

**Listen to The Opinions of The Others**
Your supervisor might give you a new job position and list all the further steps that need to be taken to get promoted. If he/she hesitates and does not agree to promote you, ask what the reason of the refusal is.

**When The Process Is Complete**
In case of negative answer, agree on the next meeting in 90 days. If you receive a positive answer, write down the details of the compensation.

# 10 Tips for picking up the right beginner-friendly telescope

Selecting your first telescope can seem daunting; however, you will be able to find the right one with these easy tips.

1. **Forget about magnification.** High magnification figures may appear attractive, but picture quality is much more important. Therefore, a clear view is always better than a blurry close-up picture.

2. **Pay attention to aperture.** Aperture means the size of the telescope’s lens or mirror. The larger the aperture, the better the telescope.

3. **Choose a simple mount.** Basic alt-azimuth mounts are usually the best option for new users. Advanced mounts may cause unnecessary issues.

4. **Think about a Dobsonian.** Such types of telescopes are compact, reliable, and affordable.

5. **Do not buy telescopes from departments.** All telescopes that look cheap in the store provide you with disappointing quality. It is better to buy a small telescope from an astronomy shop.

6. **Consider portability.** The best telescope is the one you will be taking with you. If it is too heavy to move, you will hardly use it.

7. **Remember about binoculars.** A good pair of 7x50 or 10x50 binoculars may be a great first step for you. They are easy to use and effective.

8. **Look for accessories.** Basic accessories include two eyepieces, a finder scope, and a solid mount.

9. **Use astronomy applications.** Apps like Stellarium or SkySafari may help you learn the names of the stars and planets in the first few nights.

10. **Pay attention to reality.** You shouldn’t expect that you will see the planets looking like the pictures taken by NASA. seeing Saturn’s rings or Jupiter’s moons with your own eyes is still amazing.

Start simple, keep it fun, and spend a few nights learning the sky. Your first telescope doesn’t need to be perfect—it just needs to get you outside looking up.

Hybrid learning must be perceived as a step forward in the evolution of the lecture rather than as something that brings an end to it. The lecture has been used for centuries as the way in which an expert conveys knowledge and complicated ideas to students and inspires them, thus directly stimulating their intellect. The traditional lecture, with students passively attending classes in large classrooms at a particular time, does not fully address the needs of modern students. Hybrid learning can keep the benefits of lecture while addressing its drawbacks.

The hybrid format is characterized by the combination of face-to-face teaching and online learning resources such as recorded lectures, discussion forums, online quizzes, and virtual office hours. The hybrid model offers more freedom for students, as they now have access to recorded materials that help learn complicated content at their own pace and even Continuing their studies when they are not able to attend lectures due to illness, work, or travel. It makes learning available for students with disabilities and for those who live far from universities.

There are some people who claim that the usage of the hybrid model limits the connections between the students. This argument is true, as students acquire skills through discussions and talks with their professors or other students. However, hybrid learning does not mean that universities have to abandon these techniques as well. The hybrid format allows them to use classroom hours more efficiently. Instead of repeating the materials that can be watched online, university teachers can focus on discussions and problem solving.

Thus, lectures should not be considered as one-way communication process, but rather as intellectual sharing. The role of teachers will still be significant, as they will provide students with challenging information, introduce them to complicated theories, and promote discussions. Although technology cannot change this idea fundamentally, it will be a huge support for professors.

Hybrid learning, however, will only works if it is implemented with a proper mindset, and not just used as a cheap alternative to traditional forms of learning. training, digital access, and interactive course design. If they do so, hybrid learning can make higher education more flexible, inclusive, and engaging while ensuring that the lecture remains relevant in a changing world.

The issue of rent stabilization can be defined as a controversial subject in urban policy, being marked by a multitude of economic and social trades. The theory underlying these interventions is that the unregulated housing market is not able to provide suitable housing for the poor population, which leads to a rise in the rent to unacceptable levels. However, the implementation of rent stabilization policies leads to a number of debates on this topic due to the complex nature of the results of this intervention.
This literature review will explain the complexity of rent stabilization programs by analyzing their positive results along with the unintended negative effects of these programs. 

Many studies support the idea that rent stabilization was helpful for tenants, making it impossible for landlords to raise the rent and stabilizing the essential elements of community life. Supporters of this idea point out the potential of this policy to make housing affordable and accessible for many low-income families in neighborhoods where gentrification is a common thing. They claim that by regulating housing prices, rent stabilization is able to distribute the housing resources adequately. At the same time, there are many critics who argue that this policy distorts the price signals in the housing market, discourages the construction of new housing and makes the situation even worse. The aim of this literature review is to present both points of view and combine the researches that use empirical methods to understand how rents are affected by rent stabilization.

Riding a long distance of the century needs an organized and progressive training routine. Following the 16-week training schedule, you can strengthen your heart endurance, stamina, and nutritional knowledge.

**Weeks 1-4: Basic training**
The first few weeks of training should concentrate on staying consistent. Ride your bike 3-4 times per week until it becomes habitual. Ride on weekdays for about 45 to 60 mins of moderate intesnity. The long-distance ride of the weekend should begin with 25 miles in week 1, finally finishing with 40 miles in week 4.

**Weeks 5-8: Increasing the duration and intensity**
From Week 5, start riding uphill or practice interval training at least once a week; do not forget about riding on weekdays. It is time to extend the duration of long weekend rides from 45 miles in week 5 to reach 60 miles in week 8. Use these workouts for nutritional practice while riding: aim for an intake of 30-60 grams of carbs + taking one portion of the water per hour.

**Weeks 9-12: The peak period**
During the next four weeks, keep adding rides during the weekdays and focus on reaching the maximum distance covered on Saturdays and Sundays. Plan to ride for 70 miles in week 10 and for 80-85 miles at the end of the training course. If you manage to ride 85 miles in training, youâ€™ll be able to complete the last 15 miles in a race without any extra efforts.

**Weeks 13-16: Last phase of training**
Now, concentrate on decreasing your weekly mileage to allow the muscles to recover. For example, switch to a long ride of 50 miles in week 14; during week 15 ride 30 miles. In the last week of the cycle, do 2 rides for a short distance which need to be simple and light. Make sure you have enough sleep and drink much water before the century ride.

# 10 Ways to Get Ready for Your First Sprint Triathlon

So you've made up your mind to go for a sprint triathlon—great! Don't worry if you're a beginner. Here are some reliable tips for completing your race.

**1. Plan your approach.** Find a beginner's 12-week training plan and stick to it. You'll thank yourself later.

**2. Train in swimming, cycling, and running.** These three disciplines must be practiced appropriately. Be confident in all three modes of movement before the day of the race.

**3. Get the necessary gear.** You don't need any high-end equipment, but you will benefit from getting a good bike and a pair of swimming goggles. You will be grateful in the future.

**4. Build your swimming experience.** If water terrifies you, start training in a pool. There is nothing embarrassing in taking small steps.

**5. Strength train two times a week.** Doing strength workouts on two days a week will help you avoid injuries and make things much easier.

**6. Practice transitions.** Learn how to switch from one discipline to another by practicing several times. You will discover that it is much easier to do than you thought.

**7. Pay attention to your body's feelings.** Training hard is good, but so is taking a break from training. The importance of rest days is far from being minimal, but it does not mean that one should be idle.

**8. Check everything in advance.** Your race clothes, food, gear—get accustomed to everything beforehand. The day of the race should be free of surprises.

**9. Find your tribe.** Search for a triathlon club in your area or find someone to train with. This will help you become even more motivated.

**10. Don’t ignore your anxiety.** You are going to face a great challenge, and feeling anxious is normal, means that you care about what you are going to do, which is very good.

# The Effectiveness of Facial Recognition Policies

Facial recognition technology brings forth issues regarding privacy; nevertheless, overregulation could also impede new ideas and create a legal regime that does not work.

Supporters of the agenda of creating a strict regulatory regime for the technology argue that facial recognition creates opportunities for mass surveillance and infringes civil liberties. However, it is essential to bear in mind that regulation cannot prevent motivated actors from creating or using such technologies. Authoritarian regimes and criminal organizations will use them no matter how strict the law is. Therefore, if we impose certain restrictions on the technology in democracies, we will only transfer the power of technology development to those who can act without ethical considerations.

Moreover, excessive regulation does not allow us to see how beneficial facial recognition is. Law enforcement agencies use facial recognition to identify suspects in serious crimes, find missing children, and fight human trafficking. Financial companies use it for fraud detection and secure authentication. It is also used by medical researchers to investigate genetic diseases. Thus, a strict ban on the technology will mean banning its beneficial usages as well.

The fundamental problem with regulations is that they are inflexible. Technology changes rapidly and often faster than the legislation. Instead of forming strict regulations, it is important to establish accuracy standards and transparency requirements regarding the technology usage as well as impose various accountability measures. The idea is that companies should announce the usage of the technology, and people should have some means of redress in the case their rights are infringed when the technology is applied.

Moreover, regulations differ significantly from country to country, resulting in the problem of compliance and being unable to guarantee effective privacy. A photo posted on an American social network can be analyzed using the facial recognition technology with no limitations anywhere in the world. 

Instead of looking for impossible prohibitions, it is worth explaining the rules of usage of the technology and investing into auditing practices. Regulations should define the minimum standards for the technology while allowing innovations to thrive. than regulations that drive development underground or overseas.

Companies are more commonly offering unlimited vacation time or “paid time off with discretion,” as a strategy to attract and retain talent. Unlike conventional paid time off policies that assign a fixed number of vacation days and require employees to build this leave providing system over time, unlimited vacation systems enable employees to take vacation time whenever they wish but with the employer’s approval and consideration of business needs. While supporters of these policies point out their benefits, they also admit that they can be understood differently in terms of nurturing trust, ensuring work-life balance, and aligning employees with modern time management attitudes. The competitive labor market environment makes unlimited vacation time attractive – especially for professionals and employees who want to have more control over their personal time.

Nevertheless, the nature of the correlation between unlimited vacation policies and employee retention remains complex and often obscure. Flexible paid time off can increase the satisfaction of workers due to the fact that administrative burdens that can sometimes prevent the employees from taking vacation days are removed; however, the implementation of unlimited leave policies can boost uncertainty about the amount of time off that is socially acceptable. In addition, research shows that employees working under unclear circumstances and conditions tend to take less leave even if it is their right to take more vacation days since they do not want to look less dedicated than their peers.

Moreover, the retention literature shows that pay and benefits rarely incorporate turnover. Turnover decisions are made based on job satisfaction, perceived organizational support, fairness, burnout, advancement opportunities, and relations with supervisors. by adequate staffing, explicit usage guidelines, supportive leadership, and equitable access across roles, flexible leave may strengthen employees’ perceptions that the organization values their well-being. This literature review examines the theoretical and empirical evidence surrounding unlimited vacation policies, with particular attention to their effects on employee well-being, workplace norms, perceived organizational support, and voluntary turnover intentions.

Preparing for system design interviews involves much more than just memorizing architectural designs. You should aim to develop a process for transforming vague requirements into valid and scalable designs.

To prepare for system design interviews, first study some of the key concepts like scalability, availability, consistency, latency, partitioning, replication, caching, load balancing, queues, databases and failure recovery theories. Memorizing the definitions without understanding the implications of each concept is not enough: you should know when to choose SQL or NoSQL, synchronous or asynchronous communication, and strong or eventual consistency.

Practice on various typical design problems, such as URL shortening, messaging systems, social feeds, file storage, ride sharing systems, and video services. Use the following process for each of these tasks:

1. Make sure you have fully understood the requirements and have identified the features, users, traffic patterns, data size, latency expectations, and availability goals.
2. Calculate the capacity of the system, making some rough estimates of the number of requests per second, needed storage, required bandwidth and potential growth. State any assumptions you make.
3. Define the API and the data model. Keep them as simple as possible and ensure that they meet the primary requirements.
4. Imagine the overall architecture of the service. Explain the interaction between various client systems, services, databases and other elements.
5. Define potential bottlenecks and possible failures. This includes replication, sharding, retrying, timeout, backpressure, monitoring and disaster recovery.
6. Consider trade-offs again and explain why you made decisions taken.

During your practicing, speak out loud and time yourself. Remember that interviewers will evaluate your communication and decision-making as much as your technical knowledge. Avoid going into details of implementation until you clarify the general approach to design.

Tips to Help Rescue Cats Get Used to a New Home

It is a positive experience to adopt a rescue cat. However, getting used to living in an apartment from a shelter can be difficult for your new friend. Here are 10 hints that will help your pet easily adapt to the new environment.

1. Get the cat accustomed to the "safe zone". 
At first, don’t let the cat out of its box. Initially, your pet should stay in a small, quiet place such as the bathroom with food, water, and a litter box.

2. Avoid distractions. 
Refrain from throwing any parties and making loud noises while the cat is getting accustomed to the new home.

3. Arrange for hiding spots for your new friend. 
Cats enjoy hiding when frightened, so keep the carrier open or provide your cat with a box with a blanket.

4. Place the litter box in a designated area. 
When getting accustomed to the new apartment, your cat needs to have access to the litter box anytime it feels the need to use it.

5. Secure the balcony. 
Balconies may appear to be a nice place to spend time and relax. However, it is necessary to use a cat-proof net to ensure the safety of your pet.

6. Stick to the feeding schedule. 
Try to feed the cat at the same time every day. Predictability helps rescue cats feel safe.

7. Use pheromones. 
Pheromone diffusers help alleviate fear in cats and can help them adapt to new surroundings.

8. Make sure that tight places are inaccessible for your cat. 
It is necessary to check if any small gaps may trap your cat.

9. Create upward spaces. 
Having limited space on the floor of your apartment, making your cat feel comfortable on various levels may be very helpful.

10. Allow the cat to adjust to the new place in a comfortable way.  cats adjust in hours; others take weeks. Don't force cuddles—let them come to you when they're ready. 

Be patient, give them space, and soon enough, they’ll be ruling the roost!

The print-on-demand (POD) technology has changed the entire economics of self-publishing, removing the most important barrier that prevents independent authors from entering the market: the necessity of having money in advance. In earlier days of self-publishing, authors used to spend huge sums in advance on offset print runs. That is why the authors didn't have the possibility of selling the books before the books were published. Therefore, they faced the risk of losing all their money.

POD has made it possible to publish books based on customers' orders. Consequently, this has transformed the entire publishing industry from an inventory-based business into a print-on-demand service. Authors no longer need to invest upfront or guess estimates of demand beforehand; the printing is done when a sale happens.

The revolution that has taken place has brought book publishing to writers who have been unable to afford book publishing in the past. The cost per book is higher in POD than in offset printing, thus leading to lower profit margin. By taking into consideration that the costs associated with the POD include the lack of upfront investment, the revenue finally exceeds all original expenses.

Finally, the result of the invention of POD technology has been the explosion of self-published titles as the economics of publishing has changed greatly.

The growth of e-commerce and the abundance of social networks and streaming services have changed consumer behavior in many ways. For example, the recommendation algorithm is an invention that has allowed consumers to choose goods and services with more comfort and customization. A scientific field has been devoted to studying the impact of such algorithms on the consumer, and several reviews have analyzed different topics related to recommendation systems.

Earlier studies focused mainly on practical applications of recommendation algorithms. However, recently, the topic of the impact of such algorithms on customer behavior has become more popular among academics and companies. Although algorithms generally help customers find exactly what they are looking for, questions remain about the hidden influence of algorithms on the choice of goods and services. Moreover, many works address the question of whether the algorithm is beneficial for the consumer in terms of quality of choice and diversity of choice.

While some research highlights the advantages of using recommendation algorithms for both companies and customers, questions arise about the possible negative effects of such algorithms on society and, in particular, on consumer behavior. Moreover, while many works have analyzed the impact of algorithms on the choice of goods and services, the issue of the relationship between algorithms and consumer trust remains a topic of research.

This article is a meta-analysis of several works dedicated to the theme of the impact of recommendation algorithms on consumer choice. The purpose of this article is to highlight the main ideas and arguments of the works analyzed and provide a basis for further research on the topic.

How to Ask for a Promotion After a Big Project Ships

Seeking Timing Advice

It is advisable to wait for two to four weeks after the launch of the project before requesting a meeting with your supervisor. This will give you enough time to see how things go and for the stakeholders to fully grasp the results of the undertaking. Avoid asking for the meeting immediately after the project is completed.

Preparing Evidence

In addition, it is necessary to collect all the evidence regarding the results attained by the project, including revenues, costs, and other relevant figures. It is also advisable to remember all the excellent decisions you have delivered during the work on the project and note any mentoring experiences you have. All of this is essential to prepare a compelling case for your promotion.

Preparing a Brief Statement

Furthermore, it is critical to prepare a brief statement outlining what work you have undertaken beyond your job description, what opportunities you had while leading or participating in the project, and how these experiences relate to the level of performance required for the new position. This way, you will demonstrate to the management that you have relevant skills and competencies already and only need an opportunity to prove your abilities in a higher-level position.

Arranging a Meeting

The next step is to arrange a meeting with your manager. It is unwise to interrupt someone at work, so it is best to send an e-mail requesting a meeting. In the e-mail, state your intentions clearly: ask to discuss your opportunities for career growth, and advancement. Express your gratitude for having the chance to participate in the project and demonstrate your competencies. It is essential to ask for a thirty-minute meeting to discuss your options.

Having the Conversation

Once the meeting has started, it is advisable to acknowledge the opportunities first before proceeding to the main point of the meeting. You should be ready to provide evidence of your achievements and note that you believe the time has come for you to advance to the next level. Thus, you may ask for a recommendation for the new position directly: ‘’Considering the abovementioned opportunities, I believe it is time for me to advance my career to the next level and achieve more significant goals. In my opinion, the new position will allow me to do that while contributing more to the company’s success. Do you believe it is a good time for a promotion?’’

Taking Action

If the conversation went well, and the manager has agreed to consider your request, it is advisable to set up a follow-up meeting in ninety days to review the progress and possibly promote you. In case of refusal, it is advisable to arrange a meeting to see what else you will need to do to get promoted.

# 10 Tips for choosing a beginner-friendly telescope

Buying your first telescope is a daunting experience, but here's how to make it a little easier

1. Avoid being tempted by the highest magnification. Good telescopes produce images that are bright, clear and sharp. Higher magnification often produces a brighter but more distorted image.

2. Forget about the magnification! What the object under observation needs is maximum resolution (the ability to discern detail). This is determined by the size of the objective (main) lens or mirror. Simply put, the bigger the aperture, the more light will enter the telescope, allowing you see dim objects like distant galaxies and the fine detail on planets, such as the changing seasons on Mars.

3. Get a simple mount. An alt-azimuth (up-down and left-right) mount is easiest to use, although it may be more challenging when centring objects in the field of view. A Dobsonian mount is a good type of simple altitude-azimuth mount.

4. Think about a tabletop Dobsonian telescope. These are often a great value. This style telescope is surprisingly simple to use, so it's a good value for inexperienced astronomers or even pre-teens.

5. Don't be fooled into buying a cheap telescope from a drug store or department store. You will regret it. Trust me! It's far better to buy a small, simple telescope from an astronomy dealer who can offer help and advice.

6. Portability is important. The most important thing about a telescope for a beginning stargazer is that it should be used. So, keep the portability in mind when choosing a telescope, because if the telescope is too hard to get out and set up, it will never leave the house.

7. Buy binoculars! A good pair of binoculars can be a great first optical instrument. They're simple to use, and a lot of fun.

8. Accessoires are nice, but keep it simple. You don't need a whole bunch of frills and extra gadgets, but do try to get two different magnification eyepieces, a finder scope, and a good mount.

9. Get some good astronomy software. A good software like Stellarium or Skysafari can help beginning astronomers navigate the night sky. It can save you time, headaches, and frustration.

10. Remember, the sky is beautiful on a clear night. However, your first few nights with the telescope are going to be frustrating. You may not see the planets like you see them in magazines or web sites, but you'll see something special and unique - the rings of Saturn, the clouds of Jupiter, the four large moons of Jupiter, etc.

Enjoy the view! Starting out with a simple telescope is the best way to go, so that you can learn the constellations and get more into stargazing!
