The Rise of Newsletter Writers as Trusted News Sources Essay

With news outlets losing credibility, independent newsletter writers have provided a credible alternative for people who want to be informed

These writers have amassed large followings, which has enabled them to become influential commentators on news and current affairs.

There are several reasons why newsletter writers are cornering the market on news outlets as sources of information. First, people are losing faith in the mainstream media. In addition, people are becoming more interested in receiving information from alternative sources.

In this regard, newsletter writers are answering the demand for information from credible but non-mainstream sources of information. This development has also been facilitated by the fact that newsletter writers’ contents are personalized according to their audiences’ preferences.

“People want expert opinions that they can relate to,” says media commentator Sarah Chen. “Newsletter writers do not appear as impersonal entities that one cannot connect to, as is the case with many mainstream media outlets.”

Some newsletter writers have been able to amass a large audience of followers. This has enabled them to diversify their earnings by selling subscription-based services to their followers. In this regard, newsletter writers are bypassing the need for third-party advertisers to monetize their contents. Writers who focus on specific areas of interest have benefitted immensely from newsletters as a medium since both their expertise and personalities come out clearly in their writings. Most writers also respond to questions and comments from their followers personally, establishing lasting relationships with their audiences.

However, the market for newsletters has also created some problems. The popularity of newsletters has meant that people can get their information from unsubstantiated sources. The lack of curation has also meant that some writers have taken advantage of the system by providing misleading information with no one holding them accountable. In addition, the emergence of newsletters has created challenges for traditional news outlets as writers who would have been hired in the past as journalists provide their insights directly to consumers.

This phenomenon has also resulted in a fundamental change in the media landscape. Some traditional journalists are supplementing their careers as newsletter writers alongside their mainstream media jobs. Overall, newsletters as a medium have resulted in a shift in the dynamics of the media space.

Over the centuries, the lecture has served to allow experts to impart knowledge and structure onto a subject, and to inspire generations of students. But sitting in a stuffy lecture hall, listening to a clock tick, is not conducive to education. Hybrid learning has potential to balance out the lecture's idiosyncrasies,

by allowing a more flexible approach to a subject, while maintaining that personal touch.

A hybrid model, featuring online resources as well as an in-person component, would be a good way to balance lecture's strengths and weaknesses.

Recorded portions of the class, as well as discussion boards, quizzes, and electronic office hours, would allow for a more personalized approach to the subject, while also allowing students to catch up on materials at a pace not imposed by the instructor. The online bits would also serve to accommodate those who might not be able to make it to campus, whether because of distance or hardship. Meanwhile, the in-person component, possibly featuring more discussion and exercises led by the professor or by other students, would allow for the community building and spontaneous interaction that is an important part of university education. Some decry that hybrid learning would diminish the value of the lecture, and that it would weaken the university community. And, they are not wrong- students get a lot out of interacting with their peers and professors, and having a physical classroom and regular time and place to discuss ideas is beneficial to learning.

However, hybrid learning does not force you to do away with the face-to-face interactions as some fear.

If you build the curriculum around hybrid learning's strengths, then your classroom would be more focused on discussion and exercises, where the lecture is relegated to a time to catch up on missed materials or to introduce new topics. This would help to make the lecture a more interactive and dynamic experience, instead of the one-way conversation that its been since its early days.

Hybrid learning has the potential to bring the lecture into the 21st century, while still keeping and emphasizing the traditions held dear by educators. University lecturers should continue to be a fixture in the educational landscape. While they can't be replaced by technology, they can be supplemented. Online technologies can take over the more menial aspects of teaching, and provide more opportunities for students and professors to interact. But, for this system to work, it has to be constructed around these principles, and universities need to be willing to invest the time and money to do so. Hybrid learning offers a chance to improve higher education, if we seize it.

Simply stated, the goal of rent stabilization is to ensure that the availability of housing will be sufficient to meet demand and prevent any rent hikes that could drive lower-class citizens into poverty. Nevertheless, rent stabilization is rarely a one-sided affair and is almost always subjected to heated debate between proponents and opponents. This paper will provide a discussion of the trade-offs of implementing rent stabilization by analyzing both sides’ arguments.

As mentioned above, the topic of rent stabilization is highly controversial. The primary purpose of rent stabilization is to ensure that tenants cannot be evicted or have their rent increased at the whim of the landlords. In other words, rent control aims to ensure affordability and stability for the tenants while also ensuring that landlords are not taking advantage of the desperate demand for housing. However, the opponents of rent stabilization argue that it will hurt the housing market more than help it, causing the quality of service to decrease and the supply to drop in favor of demand. This paper will analyze the validity of both arguments and provide a summary of evidence and conclusions on the topic.

Completing a 100-mile century ride is a huge milestone. It's going to take a solid training plan to get you through this 16-week journey. The following schedule will help you build the aerobic base, muscular endurance, and nutrition knowledge needed to have a successful century ride.

Weeks 1-4: Building the Foundation
Let's talk about building a base. Base building is a period of time spent riding three to four times per week with an emphasis on low-intensity steady-state (LISS) efforts on the bike. A good target for mid-week rides is 45-to-60-minute LISS efforts. For your weekend long-rides, start with a 25-mile adventure and add five miles per week to the distance.

Weeks 5-8: Increasing Volume and Intensity
Hill repeats or interval workouts should be added in this stage once per week in addition to longer (but still low-intensity) mid-week rides. For your weekend long-rides, increase the distance every week starting with 45 miles in week five. By week eight, you should be able to complete a 60-mile long-ride. You should begin practicing your on-the-bike nutrition during these long weekend adventures. Aim for 30-to-60 grams of carbohydrates and one bottle of water/electrolytes per hour.

Weeks 9-12: Peak Training
The next step is to peak your century ride training. Your mid-week workouts should still be of low intensity, but you should be able to increase the distance slightly compared to weeks one through four. However, the real focus of this stage should be on your weekend long-rides. By week 12, you should be able to complete an 80-to-85-mile long-ride. If you can complete 85 miles during your training, then the adrenaline and energy saved during the first 70 miles of your century event will propel you to the finish line.

Weeks 13-16: Taper and Event
During this stage, you will need to decrease your overall weekly mileage while increasing your overall ride intensity. The purpose of this stage is to give your body the time it needs to recover and repair itself after months of hard training. Your long-ride in week 14 should only be 50 miles, and your week 15 long-ride should only be 30 miles. In the final week before your century ride, do two short (but still easy) easy spins to keep your legs fresh. Get plenty of rest and hydration the night before your big day, and line up for your century ride with confidence!

# 10 Tips For Training For Your First Sprint Triathlon

So youve decided to participate in a sprint triathlon. The thought of it all terrifies you, but dont fret. Here are some tips to help you get across that finish line with a smile.

1. Have a proper training schedule. Find a beginners beginners 12 week training schedule and stick to it.

2. Practice all three events. Swimming, biking, and running. You need to be comfortable with all three.

3. Buy the essentials. You might want to invest in a good bike, and a pair of swimming goggles. Save your money for more important things later.

4. Learn to swim. If you aren't comfortable swimming in open water, you could always practice in a pool first.

5. Strength training. Spend two days a week working out to build strength and prevent injuries.

6. Practice transitions. You need to learn how to move from one event to the other quickly. It isn't as hard as it looks, and it will be worth it on race day.

7. Pay attention to your body. If it tells you that it needs a break, give it one.

8. Test out equipment. See what you feel most comfortable with. The day before the race try on the outfit you'll wear and eat the food you've packed. Get used to working out in it first.

9. Surround yourself with positivity. Find a local triathlon club or find a friend to do it with you.

10. Accept the fear. You're doing something amazing, and it scares you. This is completely normal.

Remember to have fun and to enjoy the experience. You're joining a diverse group of amazing people who love a challenge. Go show everyone what you're made of!

Extreme weather impacts homeowners and their values by showing people that a house is more than just a personal possession, it is a part of an eco-system. Home ownership has always been a goal for many people as it is seen as a safe place to live. However, with new extreme weather events, flood plains, fires, hurricanes, heat-waves, cold-snaps, storms, etc; the value of a home that was once a stable and secure asset, can quickly become a liability.

This dynamic can shift the mindset of some home-buyers as well as influence their purchasing decisions throughout the home-buying process. Instead of just looking at schools, square-footage, and location; buyers need to evaluate hazard-zone maps, building materials, energy-efficiency, drainage, and if the home is in a flood or fire zone. Improvements also change from just adding value to selling, to include: raising the structure of the house, hurricane shutters, solar panels, batteries, insulation, rain gardens, and AC systems. Although home ownership is still an investment, extreme weather events force some people out of their homes, some into paying more for the same square-footage, and others into upgrading their structures to stay within budget.

As such, extreme weather events force a shift in perspective on who should be in a home and where that home should be. This shift influences a change in values as what may have once been seen as a good investment, is now viewed as a threat to personal safety. Decisions have to be made individually and communally on who gets to stay in a house, who should move, what upgrades should be made, and who pays for those upgrades. Not all people have the financial security or stability to move or invest in property upgrades. In some cases, the best option may be to rent or move into a co-op community with government assistance.

In conclusion, extreme weather events force a shift in the perception of homeownership. As a result people need to expand their definition of what a home is, how a home should be built, where a home should be, and what a home means to an individual and a community.

CHICAGO -- Ten year old Tyler Chen, once an avid baseball player, decided to quit the sport all together after two years playing year round on a premier travel team. "He had to do four nights of practice and a game every weekend. He was just so tired" said his mother Sarah Chen. "He didn't see any fun in it anymore".

Pediatricians and sports psychologists are now seeing a rising epidemic of overzealous parents pushing kids to specialize in one sport while forcing them into grueling year round practices and tournaments. "There is a huge problem with overuse injuries and emotional issues like anxiety and depression due to the pressure these kids face", says Dr. Elizabeth Murray, a pediatric sports medicine specialist and pediatrician at the University of Rochester. "Kids are going through Tommy John shoulder surgeries in middle school, the same procedures once only seen in professional players. More worrying is the emotional trauma. If a child's sole focus is one sport and they get injured or have a losing season it can feel like their entire world is crashing down around them".

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that kids refrain from specializing in a single sport until at least puberty, and ideally 15 or 16. The AAP also stresses that while encouraging free play is important, participation in multiple sports is healthier and a more well-rounded approach to sports and physical activity. "Specializing at too young an age increases the risk of overuse injuries and puts unnecessary strain on growing joints and muscles", said Dr. Murray.

Children are being pushed to compete in year round leagues and tournaments for travel teams as young as age seven, pressured by parents who believe winning scholarships to junior colleges and universities will help pay for an advanced education. The U.S. sports industry is a 30 billion dollar a year business and many parents are feeling the pressure to get their kids where they need to be to succeed in the highly competitive world of youth athletics.

There is a movement among advocates to make some sports more amateur and less like professional organizations. Encouraging parents and coaches to allow kids to have fun and not overdo it. For example, Tyler now spends his afternoons riding his bike with his friends, slowly learning to appreciate the joy of physical activity.

# The Limits of Regulation of Technology

Facial recognition technology certainly involves some privacy concerns, but it should not be overly regulated since such a policy might hinder innovation and result in a poorly enforced standard.

The opponents to regulation claim that facial recognition allows for mass surveillance and is a threat to privacy, but regulation only stops those who are willing to develop such technology at any cost. Restricting this technology in democratic countries will only give way to more innovative but illegitimate facial recognition technologies in authoritarian regimes or transnational criminal organizations.

Moreover, regulation does not consider the many benefits of facial recognition technology.

It is used to identify perpetrators of heinous crimes, find abducted children, and even prevent human trafficking. It can authenticate identity in banking interactions and protect the vulnerable, such as the disabled or terminally ill, from being deceived for their life-saving medication. Thus, a blanket ban on facial recognition technology deprives law enforcement, banks, and medical facilities of valuable safeguards. Regulation is a form of control: technology developers will find a way to make software that satisfies regulators while still being a potentially dangerous tool for transnational criminals.

There is also an issue with regulation being inflexible.

Software develops at a much faster rate than most legislative documents are updated. Instead of restricting the use of facial recognition technology, lawmakers should focus on its accuracy. Technology producers should be obligated to report publicly whenever the program identifies a person. Finally, consumers must have a legal recourse if they are adversely affected by the technology. These softer limitations might be more effective at ensuring the technology is not abused.

As a matter of fact, different countries have different restrictions, so technology producers will develop workarounds for every country’s specific limitation, thus negating the effects of any given country’s laws. One’s photo on a social media website based in the US can be scanned by a facial recognition software in an authoritarian country to assess potential dissidence.

Instead of outright banning the technology, governments can impose limitations for its use in particular cases and invest in auditing to prevent abuse. Laws that effectively limit the technology’s potential for abuse will have a chilling effect on its development in technologically advanced countries but let it proliferate elsewhere. Thus, the best approach to the issues posed by the technology involve establishing a framework of acceptable cases for the use of facial recognition technology and auditing its use.

Unlimited vacation, also known as discretionary time off or flexible leave, is a concept which is seen by many companies as an attractive way to both hire and retain employees. Unlike standard vacation time, which is a set amount of days allowed per year, unlimited vacation time is, as the name suggests, unlimited. This means that employees can take as much time off of work as they feel like, provided they ask their manager for permission and it is feasible given the current workload. While at first glance, this may seem like a probable solution to the endemic retention problems in the modern workplace, the actual connection between such a system and increased rates of retention are not so straightforward.

While offering a more flexible working environment may very well lead to higher employee satisfaction and therefore higher retention, there is reason to believe that the implementation of an unlimited vacation system may very well fail in its intended purpose. On the one hand, such a system alleviates stress by reducing the amount of bureaucracy surrounding vacations and allows the employees to take as much time off as they feel like, which can be crucial for delicate situations. On the other hand, however, it can be detrimental to retention due to the ambiguity of the new rules. The employees may feel pressured to not use any vacation time at all, as asking for time off even when they really need it may make their colleagues view them as slackers. A study on the dynamics of the workplace has shown that in many cases, an employee who takes less time off than their peers will in turn take significantly more time off in the next year as the next calendar year starts with new expectations.

Another aspect which must be considered is the effect of an unlimited vacation system on the retention rates. Studies show that salaries and benefits do not play a deciding factor in an employee’s decision to stay with their company. The employees usually decide to stay or leave based on how much they like their job, how much they feel appreciated, their perception of the company’s fairness, stress levels and workload, available opportunities, and their relationships with their manager. Thus, an unlimited vacation system may be seen as an improvement in some of these areas, but is unlikely to have a major impact on the overall rate of retention. The unlimited vacation system should ideally be supplemented with additional benefits and perks, as well as proper staffing and manager training, to increase the likelihood of a positive outcome. This literature review will explore the subject of unlimited vacations and analyze the potential effects which it may have on employee wellbeing, workplace dynamics, perception of organizational support, and turnover rates.

Preparing for a system-design interview means drilling for months, memorizing scores of architectural patterns, scalability principles or solutions to common problems.

Do not try to cram for the interview. Instead, develop a repeatable process that will allow you to approach a vague problem statement and turn it into a working solution.

Review the basic concepts such as scalability, availability, consistency, latency, partitioning, replication, caching, load balancing, queues, databases, and recovery. Make sure that you know the tradeoffs between the alternatives (SQL vs NoSQL, synchronous/asynchronous, strong/eventual consistency) and can explain why one solution is better than the other in different scenarios.

Then, practice solving common problems. For each problem, try to describe the ideal system that would handle the needs of its users and customers.

Some common problems include URL shortener, chat, social media feed, file storage, ride sharing, video service, etc. Try to describe a simple example for all of these problems. Here is a sample problem: Describe a system that allows users to shorten URLs and then share them. First, outline the requirements, capacity, and constraints. What are the most important features of the system? How many users and requests per second do you expect the system to handle? What is the expected latency and SLA?

Next, describe the system’s architecture. Make sure to keep it simple and stick to the most important aspects of the problem. Next, go over the details of the implementation and identify potential bottlenecks. Think about how you will scale the system, implement replication and sharding, if needed, as well as fault tolerance, retries, timeouts, backpressure, caching, and monitoring.

Make sure to revisit the requirements and explain which constraints you have addressed. Also, highlight the tradeoffs that you have made and what would you change in the system if you needed to support more users.

When practicing in front of a mirror or with a friend, speak loud and do not forget to ask clarifying questions. The interviewer wants to know your thought process, so avoid getting stuck in any part of the solution. Also, when describing the components and API, make sure to stay high-level and show that you understand the big picture and the interactions between various parts of the system.

Avoid premature optimization and solution selection. Do not try to describe a fully working system with every edge case in mind. Instead, show that you understand the problem and can select the optimal solution based on the requirements.

In preparation for the interview, study the articles about system design and the architecture of products that you will be discussing. Remember to document your thoughts and practice the verbal description of the system’s architecture. During the interview, always ask clarifying questions and make sure to admit when you do not know something instead of pretending to be an expert.

10 Tips for introducing a rescue cat to a new apartment

Getting a new rescue cat is one of the happiest moments for any pet lover. However, getting used to the new environment may be challenging for your furriend. Here are some helpful tips on how to best break the rescue cat in a new apartment.

Make a safe zone

Do not let your cat explore the whole apartment alone at first. Make a safe area where the cat can hide if it feels threatened. You may use a separate bathroom or a bedroom.

Make sure the area is calm and without any sudden noises.

Host a party for your cat

In the first few days, avoid any noisy activities. Cats are very sensitive to disturbances, and it may take them longer to adapt to the new environment. In the meantime, you can play some calming music to cheer your cat up.

Create a safe haven for your cat

Some cats feel safest in the transport cage they arrived in. If you want to furnish the safe zone, leave a cardboard box with a soft towel for your cat to hide in.

Make sure the litter box is located in a calm place

The location should not be too crowded. If you have a loft apartment, make sure to equip each level with a litter box. However, double-check if your balcony is cat-proof. Make it secure with nets in case your cat wants to explore the outside world.

Establish a daily schedule

Cats need the daily routine to feel safe. Try not to disturb their schedule as much as possible.

Use pheromone sprays or plugins

Pheromone plugins or sprays are an incredibly useful tool in breaking a cat in a new apartment. Make sure to use them in the safe zone as much as possible. The best-selling pheromone plugin is Feliway.

Close all narrow gaps and openings

Make sure there are no narrow openings leading to dangerous places. Your cat may get stuck behind the washing machine or under the sofa in case there is a narrow space there.

Make the apartment high

Since most apartments have a small area, make it tall by adding a cat tree or a perch.

Let the cat come to you

Depending on the personality, the cat may start hugging and purring you immediately or after a couple of days. Never force the affection, let the cat come to you.

Print-on-demand (POD) technology has significantly changed the way an author can publish their book of choice. First, it removed the major obstacle to publishing books independently, which was lack of funds. Before the introduction of POD, self-publishing involved buying off-sets prints in the range of hundreds or even thousands of copies of one’s book, which was very expensive. The author had to purchase the money worth thousands of monies before they could sell a single copy of their book. With the invention of POD, the situation was completely changed. Instead of buying hundreds or thousands of papers to print one’s work, people could print one paper at a time. Thus, POD converted an expensive business of buying offsets into a cheaper venture where one could make money out of nothing. It was a sure way of earning income as it eliminated the need to speculate about the amount of books that would fail to sell.

POD has also changed the way publishers make profits on the books they print. Though it is cheaper to print books using offset printing, the costs associated with POD are lower than those involved with offset printing. This has led to a decrease in profits from POD printed materials. However, the author eliminates the risks that would have been incurred when buying offset prints wholesale. In addition, through POD, the location of a publisher is no longer a geographical constraint when selling their books.

All these changes that POD introduced to the publishing industry have brought about an increase in the number of books published independently. The reason is that before POD it was very risky to speculate on the number of books that would sell, while with POD the author needs to worry less about the amount they will earn. It has made publishing something easy to do and hence increased the supply of published works.

The proliferation of e-commerce platforms, streaming services, and social media networks has fundamentally transformed how consumers discover and select products, content, and information. At the heart of this transformation lies the recommendation algorithm—a computational system designed to predict user preferences and filter the vast array of available options into a manageable, personalized subset. As these algorithms have become increasingly sophisticated, incorporating collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, and deep learning techniques, their influence over consumer decision-making has drawn substantial scholarly attention across marketing, information systems, psychology, and computer science disciplines.

At first, people studying recommendation systems were mainly interested in how well they worked from a technical standpoint, looking at how accurate they were and how good the algorithms were. But as these systems became a bigger part of our daily lives, researchers started to think about how they affect us in a broader sense, like how they impact our behavior and thoughts. Now, people are wondering if these systems really help us by making it easier to find what we want and reducing the amount of information we have to sift through, or if they actually limit our choices and make us stick to what we already like, creating a kind of "filter bubble". At the same time, researchers are also looking at how these algorithmic recommendations interact with how much we trust them, how personalized they seem, and how often they surprise us, and how all these things together influence what we buy and how happy we are with our purchases.

There's a lot of talk about how recommendation systems affect the choices we make as consumers. Some people think these systems are helpful because they show us things we might not have found on our own. On the other hand, others are worried that if we rely too much on these algorithms, we'll lose our ability to make decisions for ourselves and end up doing the same things as everyone else. It's also a problem that we don't always know how these systems work or what's really going on behind the scenes. This lack of transparency, along with concerns about manipulation and bias, makes it hard to understand how these systems are really affecting us as consumers. For instance, are they really giving us what we want, or are they just pushing us towards certain things? Do they help us discover new things, or do they just keep showing us the same old stuff? These are important questions because they get at the heart of how much control we have over our own choices.

This study looks at how recommendation algorithms affect the choices people make when they buy things. It checks out the main ideas, what research has found, and how researchers do their studies. The goal is to figure out what everyone agrees on and what they don't, find out what we still don't know, and suggest where future research should go. This is a big deal because recommendation algorithms are becoming more and more important in how people make decisions about what to buy.

# How to Ask for a Promotion After a Big Project Ships

**Timing Matters**
Wait 2-4 weeks after project launch to request a meeting. This allows you to assess results and gives stakeholders distance to evaluate impact objectively. Avoid asking immediately—you'll appear opportunistic rather than strategic.

**Document Your Impact**
Gather concrete metrics: revenue generated, costs saved, user adoption rates, or efficiency improvements. Quantify your contributions clearly. Note leadership moments, mentorship provided, and how you solved critical problems. This isn't bragging—it's evidence.

**Prepare a Clear Narrative**
Articulate what you did beyond your job description. Explain how the project expanded your responsibilities and capabilities. Connect your growth to the next level's requirements. Show that you've already been performing at a higher level.

**Schedule Strategically**
When you want to talk to your manager about your career, it's a good idea to ask for a meeting instead of just catching them off guard. Send a simple email that says something like, "I'd like to discuss my career growth and the things I've been doing. Can we meet for 30 minutes this week?" This shows that you're professional and it gives your manager time to get ready for the meeting.

**During the Conversation**
When asking for a promotion, start by showing gratitude for the opportunities you've had so far. Talk about what you've achieved without getting defensive. For example, you could say something like "I'm proud of what we accomplished with the last project - it was finished on time and under budget, and I was in charge of making sure all the different teams worked together." Then, be straightforward and ask for what you want: "Given my accomplishments, I think I'm ready to move up to a new role, like [position]. What do you think about that?

**Listen to Feedback**
Your manager may say yes, outline next steps, or identify gaps. If they hesitate, ask what's needed: "What would help me get there?" Take notes and create an action plan.

**Follow Up**
If the answer is no, schedule a 90-day check-in. Continue demonstrating value and addressing feedback. If yes, confirm details in writing.

Asking for a promotion isn't about thinking you deserve one - it's about showing that you've taken on more work and should be recognized for it. When you do it the right way, it can actually help your career move forward.

# 10 Tips for choosing a beginner-friendly telescope

Getting your first telescope can be a bit overwhelming, but don't worry, it's not as complicated as it seems. To make things easier, we've put together a list of 10 easy-to-follow tips to help you choose a telescope that's right for you and that you'll really enjoy using.

1. **Don't fall for the "highest magnification" trap.** What really matters is the quality of the image, not how much it's zoomed in. A clear and steady picture is always better than a blurry one that's too close up.

2. **Start with the aperture**. The aperture is basically the size of the telescope's main lens or mirror. A bigger aperture means it can collect more light, which makes it easier to spot the Moon, planets, and really faint objects in the sky.

3. **Get started with a simple mount**. For beginners, a sturdy alt-azimuth mount is the way to go - it's easy to use because it just moves up and down, and left and right. The thing with complicated mounts is they can be a real pain to set up, which can be frustrating when you're just starting out.

4. **Think about a tabletop Dobsonian telescope**. These small reflector telescopes are usually pretty cheap and really stable, making them easy to use. They're perfect for both kids and grown-ups who want to explore the night sky.

5. **Steer clear of department-store telescopes**. Those super-cheap ones with wobbly tripods and fancy packaging can be a letdown. Instead, opt for a smaller, high-quality scope from a trusted astronomy store - it's a much better bet.

6. **Portability matters**. The perfect telescope is one that you'll actually use, not one that's stuck in a closet because it's too heavy or a hassle to move around. If you can't easily carry it outside, it's unlikely you'll bother, and that means it'll just collect dust.

7. **Don't forget binoculars** - they're a great way to start exploring the night sky. A good pair, like 7x50 or 10x50, is easy to use and can be really fun for stargazing. You'll be surprised at how much you can see with them.

8. **Take a closer look at what comes with it.** You'll want the essentials, like a couple of eyepieces, a finder scope, and a mount that won't topple over. Don't worry if it doesn't come with a ton of extra stuff - you can always add more later.

9. **Get started with astronomy apps**. If you're new to stargazing, apps like Stellarium or SkySafari can be a huge help. They can show you what's out there in the night sky, from stars and planets to constellations. This makes it way less overwhelming when you're just starting out and looking up at the stars for the first time.

10. ** Set realistic expectations.** Planets won’t look like NASA photos, but seeing Saturn’s rings or Jupiter’s moons with your own eyes is still amazing.

Start simple, keep it fun, and spend a few nights learning the sky. Your first telescope doesn’t need to be perfect—it just needs to get you outside looking up.

Stores used to be places where you'd go and actually talk to people, like the cashier. It was a chance to catch up with your neighbors or just say hello to someone. But now, with self-checkout systems, all of that is changing. These machines are taking the place of human cashiers, making the shopping experience more about efficiency than actual human connection. When you use self-checkout, you're not just buying stuff, you're also doing the work that a cashier used to do. It's like you're a part of the store's team, but without the chat and the smile. This shift is pretty big, and it's changing the way we think about stores and how we interact with them. What does this mean for us, and for the stores we shop at? Is it all about speed and convenience, or is there something more to it?

This change is a mixed bag, giving people more control over their shopping experience, but also making them feel disconnected. On the one hand, self-checkout is great for people who want to get in and out quickly, don't like talking to others, and prefer to use technology to do their own thing. It's like a quiet, easy way to leave a store without having to deal with the awkwardness of small talk, which can be really stressful for some people.

When you use the self-checkout lane, something changes. You start to feel like you're being watched all the time. There are cameras above you, sensors that check the weight of what you're buying, and red lights that blink at you. This makes the store feel less welcoming. Instead of feeling like a customer, you start to feel like you might be trying to steal something. If something goes wrong with the scan, a robotic voice stops the whole process and a store employee has to come over. This makes you feel like you're not trusted, like you might be a shoplifter. It's a pretty big shift from feeling like you're a valued customer to feeling like you're a potential problem.

When you use self-checkout, it takes away the friendly feeling you get from shopping. Stores save money on workers, but they also lose the loyalty of their customers. When you're checking out, it's just you and a machine - it's not like talking to a person. The store doesn't feel like a part of the community anymore, it's just a place to grab what you need and go. You're not getting any help or service, you're just using a machine to pay for your stuff. It's like the store is just a big warehouse, not a place where people go to shop and talk to each other.

These writers are really good at telling stories and sharing their thoughts on all sorts of things - politics, technology, and more. And the best part is, they're building a loyal following of readers who look forward to hearing what they have to say.

But newsletters are different - they send you the stuff you want to read, right to your inbox. And the best part is, you choose to get them, so it's like a relationship based on trust, not just some computer program deciding what you should see.

"According to media analyst Sarah Chen, people are craving expertise that's easy to grasp. She believes that writers of newsletters bring a unique blend of context and personality to the table, something that's often missing from mainstream media outlets."

Prominent newsletter writers have built substantial influence. Platforms like Substack have democratized publishing, allowing writers to monetize directly through reader subscriptions rather than relying on advertising or institutional backing. Writers covering politics, economics, science, and culture now command audiences rivaling traditional publications.

The success reflects several factors. Newsletter writers often specialize deeply in niche topics, developing genuine expertise. They typically maintain a consistent voice and perspective, allowing readers to understand where they stand rather than wondering about institutional biases. This approach shows that newsletters aren't meant to replace the old way of doing things, but rather work together with it.

Learning in a university setting is changing, and hybrid learning is the way forward. For a long time, lectures have been a great way for experts to share complex ideas, organize information, and motivate students. But let's be honest, the old way of doing things - where students just sit and listen in a crowded room at a set time - doesn't really work for today's students. Hybrid learning is a way to keep the good things about lectures, like the interaction with the teacher and fellow students, while also making it more flexible and effective. It's not about getting rid of lectures altogether, but about making them better suited to the needs of modern students.

Hybrid learning is a great way to study because it mixes classroom teaching with online tools. This means students can learn in a way that fits their lifestyle. They can watch recorded lectures, join online discussions, take quizzes, and even meet with teachers virtually. This approach gives students more freedom to learn at their own pace, which is really helpful when they're struggling with a concept or can't make it to class. It's also a big plus for students with disabilities or those who live far away from campus, as it makes education more accessible to them. With hybrid learning, students can review material whenever they want, which is especially useful when they're ill, working, or commuting. Overall, it's a more flexible way to learn, and that's a big advantage.

People think that online classes can hurt the sense of community that makes university life special. And that's a fair point - students learn a lot from talking to teachers and other students, not just from the course material. But that doesn't mean universities have to give up on those experiences. Hybrid learning actually helps make the most of classroom time. Instead of lecturers repeating stuff that students could watch online, they can use in-person time for discussions, solving problems, lab work, case studies, and giving feedback. This way, students can still have those important face-to-face interactions. By doing it this way, universities can make sure students get the best of both worlds - the flexibility of online learning and the benefits of in-person learning.

The future of lectures should be more like a conversation, not just a one-way talk. Professors are still crucial, but not just for sharing information - they should also challenge students' thoughts, explain tough concepts, and lead meaningful discussions. Technology can't replace what professors do, but it can definitely help. It's about working together to create a richer learning experience. Professors will guide students, and technology will support that process. This way, students will get more out of the lecture, and it will be a more shared experience.

Hybrid learning works best when it's done right, not just used as a quick fix. To make it really work, universities need to put in the time and money to train their teachers, make sure everyone has access to the right technology, and create interactive classes that keep students interested. If they do all this, hybrid learning can make college more flexible, so it's easier for everyone to learn, and more engaging, while still keeping the traditional lecture relevant in today's fast-changing world.

Rent stabilization programs, designed to mitigate housing affordability crises and protect tenants from displacement, represent a contentious area of urban policy with a complex array of economic and social trade-offs. The foundational rationale for such interventions rests on the premise that unregulated housing markets can fail to provide adequate, affordable housing, particularly for low-income households, leading to exploitative rent increases and reduced housing security. However, the implementation of rent stabilization is rarely without consequence, generating vigorous debate among policymakers, economists, and housing advocates regarding its efficacy and long-term impacts. This literature review aims to explore the multifaceted trade-offs inherent in rent stabilization programs, examining both the intended benefits and the often-unintended drawbacks.

Rent control is a big deal for people who rent homes. It helps keep rents from getting too high and makes sure people aren't forced to move out of their neighborhoods. Supporters say it makes housing more affordable, especially in areas where a lot of new people are moving in and prices are going up fast. But others argue that rent control can actually make things worse by messing with the housing market, stopping new homes from being built, and making landlords less likely to take care of their properties. This can even lead to a shortage of homes and make the ones that are available worse quality. We're going to take a closer look at both sides of the argument and see what the research says about how rent control affects rents, the number of homes available, property values, what landlords do, and how it impacts people who rent. By looking at all the evidence, we hope to get a better understanding of the trade-offs that come with rent control and where experts agree and disagree.

Doing a 100-mile bike ride is a big deal. It takes a lot of planning and training to get ready for it. You need to build up your endurance and strength over time. This usually takes around 16 weeks. During this time, you'll work on getting your heart and muscles ready for the challenge. You'll also learn how to eat and take care of yourself to make sure you have the energy you need to finish the ride.

**Weeks 1–4: Building the Base**
To get the most out of your training, it's essential to be consistent and establish a routine. Try to ride three or four times a week. For your mid-week rides, aim for 45 to 60 minutes at a moderate pace - this will help you build up your endurance. The weekend long ride is a crucial part of your training. Start with 25 miles in Week 1 and gradually increase the distance by 5 miles each week. By Week 4, you should be able to ride 40 miles. This will help you make steady progress and improve your overall performance. Remember, consistency is key, so try to stick to your routine as much as possible.

**Weeks 5–8: Increasing Volume and Intensity**
To boost your leg strength, try adding hill climbs or interval training to your routine once a week. For your mid-week rides, keep them engaging but not too demanding. As for your weekend long rides, aim to increase the distance from 45 miles in Week 5 to 60 miles by Week 8. It's also a good idea to practice fueling while you're on the bike during these longer rides - try to consume between 30 to 60 grams of carbs and drink one bottle of water or electrolytes every hour. This will help you build endurance and get your body used to what it needs to perform at its best.

**Weeks 9–12: Peak Mileage**
As you get closer to the event, this block will help you prepare for the physical challenges you'll face. You'll notice your mid-week riding will pick up a bit, and your long weekend rides will be the toughest. By Week 10, aim to hit around 70 miles, and by Week 12, try to reach a peak ride of 80 to 85 miles. If you can handle 85 miles comfortably during training, the excitement and energy of the event - plus the help of drafting - will carry you through the last 15 miles on the big day.

**Weeks 13–16: Tapering and Event Day**
As you get closer to your big event, it's time to start easing up on your training. So, for Week 14, try to cut back your long ride to 50 miles, and then in Week 15, bring it down to 30 miles. For the last week, just do a couple of short, easy rides to keep your legs loose. Make sure you're getting plenty of sleep and drinking lots of water - this will help your muscles recover and rebuild. By the time you line up for your century ride, you'll be feeling strong and ready to go.

# 10 Tips for Training for Your First Sprint Triathlon

You've taken the first step by deciding to give a sprint triathlon a shot - that's great news! If you're new to all this, don't worry, we've got you covered. Here are some really helpful tips that will guide you through your training and get you feeling like a total rockstar when you cross that finish line.

**1. Start with a plan.** Find a beginner-friendly 12-week training schedule and actually follow it. You'll thank yourself later.

**2. Master all three disciplines.** To succeed, you need to be proficient in swimming, cycling, and running - there's no picking and choosing. Make sure you're comfortable with each discipline before the big day, it'll make all the difference.

**3. Invest in the basics.** You don't need fancy gear, but a decent bike and swim goggles are worth the money. Your future self will appreciate it.

**4. Build your swimming confidence.** If you're nervous about open water, do some practice swims in a pool first. There's no shame in starting small.

**5. Don't skip strength training.** It's really important to do strength exercises at least two days a week. This helps prevent injuries and makes everyday activities a lot easier. It's a win-win situation - you'll be safer and stronger, which is a great combination.

**6. Nail your transitions.** Practice switching between sports multiple times. It's surprisingly tricky and easier than you'd think to improve on.

**7. Listen to your body.** Training hard is great, but recovery matters just as much. Rest days aren't lazy—they're essential.

**8. Try everything out before the big day.** Make sure you've worn your racing gear, eaten your usual breakfast, and set up your equipment just like you will on race day. You don't want any surprises when it really counts.

**9. Find your people.** Join a local triathlon club or find training buddies. The support and motivation are invaluable.

**10. Embrace the nerves.** You're doing something legitimately challenging. A little nervousness means you care—that's totally normal and actually pretty cool.

You've made it this far, so have faith in your abilities and the hard work you've put in. Consistency is key, and recalling what drove you to start this journey can be a great motivator. You're on the verge of becoming part of a fantastic group of like-minded individuals who share your passion for triathlons. So, go out there and give it your all - you're ready for this!

Extreme weather is changing the way we think about owning a home. For a long time, having a house was seen as a stable and secure investment. But now, with floods, wildfires, and hurricanes happening more often, that's not always the case. A house can quickly lose its value if it's in a dangerous area, or if insurance becomes too expensive. And if the roads, power, and water systems in the area keep failing, it can be really tough for homeowners. This is a big shift from the past, when owning a home was seen as a key part of being independent and financially secure. Now, people are realizing that their homes are part of a bigger environmental system, and that can be a pretty vulnerable thing.

When looking for a home, buyers are now considering things like flood zones, areas prone to wildfires, and how well the house is built to withstand natural disasters. They're also thinking about things like energy efficiency and access to reliable utilities, in addition to the usual factors like school districts and the size of the house. Making homes more resilient to extreme weather is becoming a priority, with features like elevated foundations, fire-resistant roofs, and storm shutters no longer being seen as luxuries in many areas. Some people are even installing backup power systems, extra insulation, and cooling systems to help keep their homes safe and comfortable. However, not everyone has the same ability to adapt to these changes. Wealthier homeowners may be able to afford to retrofit their homes or move to a safer area, but lower-income families may be stuck in dangerous areas, facing higher insurance costs or even losing their homes. This can create a big divide between those who can afford to protect themselves from extreme weather and those who can't.

Extreme weather is changing the way we think about owning a home. It's not just about individual success, but also about the community's role in keeping us safe. This includes decisions on where to build homes, how to prepare for emergencies, and how to deal with climate change. Communities need to figure out who will pay for protections like seawalls or flood-proof buildings, and how to help people who can't just pick up and move. In areas that get hit by disasters over and over, it might be more practical for people to rent, live in cooperative housing, or get help from the government to relocate rather than trying to own a traditional home.

**CHICAGO** — Ten-year-old Tyler Chen used to love baseball. But after two years of playing year-round on a premier travel team, practicing four nights a week, and traveling every weekend, the young pitcher decided to quit sports entirely.

"Sarah Chen, his mom, said he was just worn out," she explained. The fun had disappeared.

More and more kids are going through what Tyler did. Doctors who specialize in kids' health and sports psychologists are sounding the alarm about a big problem: a lot of kids are getting burned out from playing sports too intensely at a really young age. This happens when they focus on just one sport and don't play any others. It's becoming a pretty common issue.

Parents are signing up their kids for sports programs all year round, starting as young as seven years old. They're doing this because they want their kids to get college scholarships and be part of the huge youth sports industry, which is worth $30 billion. But experts are saying that this approach is actually not working out as planned. By pushing kids to focus so much on sports at such a young age, parents might be doing more harm than good.

"Sports injuries are on the rise, and it's not just physical harm we're talking about. Dr. Elizabeth Murray, a specialist in pediatric sports medicine, says we're seeing a lot of overuse injuries, like Tommy John shoulder surgeries, in kids as young as middle school age - something that used to only happen to professional athletes. But what's even more worrying is the impact on their mental health. Kids are feeling stressed, anxious, and depressed, and it's often because their whole sense of self is tied up in one sport. When they have a bad game or get hurt, it can feel like their whole identity is falling apart. It's like they're having an identity crisis, and that's a heavy burden for a kid to carry."

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends that children delay specialization until at least puberty, ideally age 15 or 16. The AAP emphasizes that playing multiple sports actually builds better overall athletes, prevents injury, and keeps physical activity fun.

Currently, 70% of children quit organized sports by age 13, according to the National Alliance for Youth Sports.

As kids' sports get more serious, people are telling parents and coaches to let them just have fun and take breaks. For kids like Tyler, it took a tough experience to learn this. Now, he spends his afternoons riding bikes with friends from the neighborhood, and he's slowly remembering how much fun it is to just be active and play without any pressure. He's finding joy in simple things again.

# The Limits of Facial Recognition Regulation

While facial recognition technology presents legitimate privacy concerns, excessive regulation risks stifling innovation and creating a regulatory framework that ultimately proves ineffective.

Some people think that strict rules are needed to control facial recognition because it can be used to watch everyone and hurt our freedom. But they're missing a big point: just making rules won't stop people who really want to use this technology from doing so. Places with strict control and criminal groups will keep making and using these tools no matter what laws are in place. If we make too many rules about facial recognition in countries that are free, we're just giving an advantage to people who don't care about doing the right thing.

Tight rules on facial recognition can be a problem because they don't consider the good it can do. For example, police use it to find suspects in serious crimes, locate missing kids, and stop human trafficking. Banks use it to prevent fraud and keep accounts secure. Doctors even use it to study genetic disorders. If we ban it completely, we'll get rid of the bad uses, but also the good ones.

The thing with rules is they can be too strict. Technology is always changing, and laws can't keep up. Instead of making rules that will soon be outdated, we should focus on making sure things are accurate, transparent, and accountable - and that these standards can adapt as technology advances. When companies use facial recognition, they should let people know, and if something goes wrong, individuals should have some recourse - but that doesn't mean we need to get rid of the technology altogether. We just need to make sure it's used responsibly.

Facial recognition rules are all over the place, and that's a big problem. Imagine you post a picture on social media in the US - it can still be used for facial recognition anywhere in the world, without any limits. This doesn't really help keep your personal info private, it just makes things complicated for companies to follow the rules.

Instead of trying to ban things that are impossible to stop, lawmakers should create clear rules for how things can be used and make sure there are ways to check that these rules are being followed. Rules work best when they set basic standards and let new ideas happen. When it comes to recognizing faces, having fewer rules will actually help keep people's privacy safe better than having strict rules that just make people work on these things in secret or in other countries. This way, we can make sure that new technologies are used in a way that respects people's privacy. By setting clear guidelines, we can help companies use face recognition technology in a responsible way, which is better than trying to stop it completely.

Companies are now offering unlimited vacation time as a way to attract and keep top talent. This means employees can take time off when they need it, as long as their manager agrees and it doesn't hurt the business. It's different from traditional vacation time, where you get a set number of days off and have to earn them over time. With unlimited vacation, employees can take a break whenever they want, which can be really appealing to people who want more control over their work-life balance. This kind of policy shows that the company trusts its employees and is willing to give them the flexibility they need. In today's competitive job market, offering unlimited vacation time can be a big selling point, especially for workers who value autonomy and flexibility. It's a way for companies to stand out and show that they care about their employees' well-being. By giving employees more freedom to manage their time, companies can promote a better work-life balance and increase job satisfaction. This can be especially important for certain types of workers, like knowledge workers, who often have a lot of control over their work and value flexibility. Overall, unlimited vacation policies can be a win-win for both employees and employers, as they can help attract and retain top talent and improve overall job satisfaction.

The connection between unlimited vacation time and keeping employees is more complicated than it seems. On one hand, having flexible leave can make employees happier because it gives them the freedom to take care of personal things, family, and health issues without a lot of red tape. But on the other hand, unlimited vacation policies can create confusion. Employees might not know how much time off is okay to take, especially in workplaces where everyone is really busy or where there aren't enough staff. Studies on what's considered normal in the workplace show that when expectations are unclear, employees tend to take less time off than they would if they knew exactly how much they were allowed. This is especially true if they're worried about looking less dedicated than their coworkers. So, an unlimited vacation policy can work differently depending on the company culture, how managers behave, how much work needs to be done, whether employees feel safe to speak up, and whether leaders take time off themselves.

When it comes to keeping employees, pay and benefits aren't the only things that matter. What really makes a difference is how happy people are with their jobs, whether they feel supported by their organization, and if they think things are fair. Burnout, chances to move up, and how they get along with their bosses also play a big role. So, offering unlimited vacation time might not be enough on its own to keep people from leaving - it needs to be part of a bigger plan. If a company also makes sure it has enough staff, sets clear rules for taking time off, has leaders who care, and makes sure everyone can take advantage of the policy, it can make employees feel like their well-being matters. This study looks at what research says about unlimited vacation policies, including how they affect how employees feel, what's considered normal at work, whether employees feel supported, and whether they're likely to quit.

Preparing for a system-design interview requires more than memorizing architectures. Focus on developing a repeatable process for turning ambiguous requirements into practical, scalable designs.

Start by reviewing core concepts: scalability, availability, consistency, latency, partitioning, replication, caching, load balancing, queues, databases, and failure recovery. Understand the trade-offs rather than memorizing definitions. Be able to explain when you would choose SQL versus NoSQL, synchronous versus asynchronous communication, and strong versus eventual consistency.

Practice common design problems, such as URL shorteners, messaging systems, social feeds, file storage, ride-sharing platforms, and video services. For each problem, work through the same framework:

1. Clarify requirements. Identify key features, users, traffic patterns, data size, latency expectations, and availability goals.
2. Estimate capacity. Make rough calculations for requests per second, storage, bandwidth, and growth. State assumptions clearly.
3. Define the API and data model. Keep them simple and aligned with the main use cases.
4. Draw the high-level architecture. Explain how clients, services, databases, caches, queues, and external systems interact.
5. Explore bottlenecks and failures. Discuss replication, sharding, retries, timeouts, backpressure, monitoring, and disaster recovery.
6. Revisit trade-offs. Explain why your choices satisfy the requirements and what you would change at greater scale.

10 Tips for introducing a rescue cat to a new apartment

Getting a new cat from a shelter is a wonderful thing. It's like giving them a second chance at a happy life. But let's be real, moving from a shelter to a new home can be super scary for them. So, how can you make this big change easier for your new pet? Here are some simple tips to help your cat feel at home and relaxed in their new space.

**1. Start with a "safe zone"**
Don’t give them run of the whole place right away. Start them off in a small, quiet room (like a bathroom or bedroom) with their food, water, and litter box.

**2. Keep it quiet**
Hold off on hosting a housewarming party. Keep the noise down for the first few days so your cat doesn't get spooked by sudden sounds.

**3. Provide hiding spots**
Cats love to hide when they’re unsure. Leave their carrier open, or set up a cardboard box with a comfy blanket inside.

**4. Keep the litter box accessible**
Place the litter box in a quiet, low-traffic spot. If you have a multi-story loft, you might need one on each level at first.

**5. Cat-proof your balcony**
Apartment balconies are great, but safety first! Ensure your balcony is fully enclosed with cat-safe netting before letting your kitty join you outside.

**6. Stick to a routine**
Feed them at the same times every day. Predictability helps rescue cats feel secure.

**7. Use pheromones**
Plug in a synthetic pheromone diffuser (like Feliway) in their safe room. It mimics natural calming scents and works like magic.

**8. Block tight spaces**
Keep an eye out for tight spots, like the gap behind the washing machine or under heavy furniture, where pets might get wedged in. You'd be surprised how easily they can slip into these tiny spaces and get stuck.

**9. Go vertical**
Apartments have limited floor space, so go vertical! A tall cat tree or window perch gives them a safe lookout spot.

**10. Let them set the pace**
Some cats adjust in hours; others take weeks. Don't force cuddles—let them come to you when they're ready.

Just give them some time and space, and before you know it, they'll be in charge.

The way authors publish their own work has changed a lot thanks to print-on-demand. Before, self-publishing was a big risk because you had to pay for a lot of books to be printed at once, without knowing if they would sell. This meant spending thousands of dollars upfront, which was a huge obstacle for many writers. They would have to store all these books somewhere, and often ended up with boxes of unsold copies. But now, with print-on-demand, authors don't have to worry about that anymore. They can just print and sell books as they go, which makes it much easier for independent authors to get their work out there. This has really leveled the playing field and given more writers a chance to share their work with the world.

Printing books used to be a big risk for publishers - they had to guess how many copies to print and hope they would sell. But then POD technology came along and changed everything. Now, books are printed one at a time, only when a customer actually orders one. This has made publishing a lot more flexible and less expensive. Authors don't have to worry about predicting how many books will sell or paying for a big print run upfront. Instead, the book is printed after the sale is made, and the costs are taken out of the money the author earns. It's a much simpler and more efficient way to do things.

The rise of self-publishing has made it possible for writers to get their books out there without needing a lot of money. This is because the old way of printing books, which required a big upfront investment, is no longer the only option. Now, with print-on-demand, writers can print and sell books as they are ordered, which means they don't have to worry about storing a bunch of unsold copies. While it's true that the cost of printing each book is a bit higher with print-on-demand, the fact that writers don't have to pay for a big batch of books upfront more than makes up for it. Plus, print-on-demand works really well with online stores, making it easy for writers to sell their books all over the world without having to store them in a physical warehouse. This has been a game-changer for writers who want to get their work out to readers.

The long-term effect has been an explosion in the sheer volume of self-published titles, as the financial calculus shifted from "can I afford to publish this book" to "will anyone buy it," fundamentally lowering the stakes of creative and entrepreneurial risk-taking in publishing.

As suburban populations grow, local governments are facing mounting pressure to expand public transit beyond traditional city centers. New housing developments, crowded roads and longer commutes have intensified calls for reliable bus and rail service in communities that were once designed primarily for cars.

People who support better public transportation say that investing in it is crucial for managing growth in a way that's good for everyone. In suburbs that are growing really fast, not having many transportation options can leave people who don't have cars - like older adults, students, and people with lower incomes - cut off from things they need like jobs, schools, and medical care. Having better public transportation can also help reduce traffic jams and make it possible to build more homes and businesses near train and bus stations.

Finding the money to pay for it all is still a big problem. Suburban transit agencies usually get their funds from a mix of local taxes, grants from the state, and help from the federal government - and all of these can change suddenly. This is different from big cities that already have transit systems in place and have a steady flow of money coming in. Many suburban areas are starting from nothing, having to build their transit routes and facilities from the ground up.

Some local leaders think that raising sales taxes, creating special districts to fund specific projects, and teaming up with private companies can help pay for expansion plans. Others are looking to get money from the federal government to buy electric buses, make bus stops better, and add more rail lines. People who support these ideas say that spending money now can lead to big economic benefits later, like bringing in new businesses and increasing the value of properties near transportation routes.

Some people are against these new systems because they don't think they'll get enough people to use them to make them worth the cost. They're worried that big projects will just lead to higher taxes without really getting people to stop driving, especially in areas where not many people live.

## How to ask for a promotion after a big project ships

When? Wait at least two or three weeks after it ships. Get the metrics, then set up a meeting with your manager. Don’t ask right after it ships. It looks opportunistic. Instead, give stakeholders time to see the impact.

Write down the impact. What metrics did you achieve? Revenue? Costs saved? User adoption? Efficiency gains? Highlight moments where you led or mentored. Show what you did to solve key problems. Don’t just list things you did, write down how they contributed to the business.

Explain how you went above and beyond your regular responsibilities. Did you take ownership of new tasks? Did you lead others? Did you handle new challenges? Make sure to explain how these projects and experiences have prepared you for the next level.

Set up a meeting with your manager. Don’t catch them at the coffee machine. Send them an email saying something like, “I’d like to discuss my career goals and contributions to the company. Could we find time this week to meet?” This tells them you’re serious about talking about your career and that you need their time to do it.

Start the conversation by thanking your manager for the opportunities you’ve had. Then share your accomplishments without being defensive or self-deprecating. For example: “The project was delivered on time and under budget. I took ownership of the project and coordinated between teams to ensure its success.” Then ask: “I feel like I’m ready to take on more responsibility. I think I’m ready to be promoted to [title]. What do you think?”

Hear out your manager’s response. They might say yes, give you a timeline, or tell you what needs to happen before you can be considered. If they say no, ask: “What can I do to get to the next level?” Write down everything they say. Then come up with a plan for how to get there.

If you get a no, follow up with another meeting in 90 days. Keep doing good work and continue to work towards your goals. If you get a yes, send them an email confirming the promotion.

Asking for a promotion is not entitled. It’s showing that you are deserving of advancement due to the extra work you’ve done. Ask professionally, and you’ll be well on your way to getting the promotion you deserve.

# 10 tips to help you choose a beginner telescope

There are a lot of questions to ask when buying a telescope, and it can feel overwhelming. Here are 10 tips to help you narrow down your options.

1. Don’t get obsessed with magnification. Many people think that higher magnification means a better telescope. But image quality, determined mostly by aperture, is far more important than magnification.

2. Get an aperture you can afford. The aperture (the diameter of the telescope’s primary lens or mirror) determines how much light the telescope collects. The bigger the aperture, the brighter the view of the Moon, planets, and faint deep-sky objects.

3. Choose a simple mount. Many beginners prefer a standard alt-azimuth mount, which allows the telescope to move up and down and left and right. Some people want more complex mounts, but it can be frustrating to set up a telescope on such a mount.

4. Consider a tabletop Dobsonian. Small, tabletop Dobsonian telescopes are relatively inexpensive, stable, and easy to aim. They’re great for both kids and adults.

5. Skip the department store telescopes. Department store telescopes often come with flimsy tripods and fancy packaging, but they typically produce poor-quality images. It’s usually better to buy a smaller, well-built scope from an astronomy retailer.

6. Think about portability. A big, expensive telescope might seem cool, but if you don’t have room for it or it’s too difficult to carry, you won’t use it. A telescope you actually take outside will be much more satisfying.

7. Try binoculars first. A pair of decent 7×50 or 10×50 binoculars can be a great way to start observing. They’re easy to use and very popular among amateur astronomers.

8. Check what’s included. Most beginner telescopes come with a couple of eyepieces, a finder scope, and a mount. You don’t need any special equipment when you’re starting out.

9. Download an astronomy app. A free smartphone or tablet app like Stellarium or SkySafari will help you navigate the night sky and learn the constellations. This will make those early nights outside much easier.

10. Have realistic expectations. When you first look through a telescope, the view won’t look like the Hubble Space Telescope images. But there are plenty of celestial objects worth checking out. The sight of Saturn’s rings or Jupiter’s four largest moons will still impress you.

Keep it simple, have fun, and spend a few nights getting familiar with the night sky. Your first telescope doesn’t have to be perfect. It just has to inspire you to look up.

Newsletter writers have become major news sources

Independent newsletter writers are increasingly important commentators in the world of media, according to some analysts.

These writers are reaching large audiences and shaping the public’s understanding of current events, some analysts said.

Many independent newsletter writers have developed large, dedicated followings online.

Some newsletter writers have found ways to monetize their work directly.

These writers don’t rely on ad revenue or institutional support to pay their bills.

This means that these writers are accountable primarily to their readers, not to their employers.

The writers have carved out niche areas where they have expertise and authority.

Newsletter writers also tend to have a distinct perspective or point of view, which means that their readers know where they stand.

That’s an important part of why they’ve been so successful.

It also helps that these writers typically maintain closer relationships with their readers through comments and feedback.
