And even though many newsletter writers are very talented and knowledgeable, they still face challenges when it comes to audience growth.

This isn’t surprising, since many readers will stick with familiar sources, such as established news organizations.

But despite the challenges, newsletter writers will likely continue to be key players in the media landscape for years to come.

The lecture has been the cornerstone of higher education for hundreds of years. Experts and scholars use the lecture to introduce new concepts, structure information, and stimulate thinking. It is the primary way that a lecturer gets across important ideas to a large audience. Nevertheless, the standard method, in which students sit in a large room listening to a teacher speak for a period of time, does not cater well to today's students. While some aspects of the lecture will need to change, hybrid learning provides a solution to the current system. Hybrid learning merges on-campus instruction with digital materials such as video recordings of lectures, discussion forums, online tests and online office hours. With this system, students have more freedom. The ability to record lectures enables students to revisit topics they found challenging, study at their own speed or watch lectures at home if they were unable to attend because of sickness, employment or travel. Hybrid learning also benefits disabled students and those who live a long distance from campus. Some opponents of online education maintain that by using technology, students lose the feeling of belonging to the university environment. Although this argument is correct to a certain extent, it is important to acknowledge that learning takes place not only through lectures but also through class discussions, group activities and social interaction with classmates and teachers. However, hybrid learning does not have to mean losing out on any of these opportunities. In fact, the online format frees up classroom time to be utilised more efficiently. Teachers no longer have to repeat information that students could watch online, meaning that lecturers have more time to spend on debates, problem-solving, experiments, case studies and providing feedback. As a result, the lecture will change from being a solitary experience into something of a collaborative effort. Lecturers will still be vital to the process, not simply delivering information but also pushing students to think, explaining difficult concepts, and encouraging open dialogue. Although digital learning tools are useful, they cannot replace the expertise and insight of a lecturer. To benefit from hybrid learning, however, it must not just be introduced without careful planning, and universities should not simply offer it as a low-cost alternative to on-campus classes. Universities should allocate funds to provide staff training, ensure access to technology, and develop high-quality courses. If these steps are taken, then hybrid learning can provide a more adaptable, accessible and interesting educational experience, allowing the lecture to survive and thrive in a modern world.

In recent years, rent stabilization programs have been proposed as a solution to a myriad of problems associated with urban housing. Rent stabilization programs are typically put forward as measures aimed at solving two related problems: the affordability problem and the problem of tenant displacement. However, any attempt to mitigate either of these problems is not without tradeoffs, resulting in various economic and social consequences that are not always desirable. Consequently, many people are divided on whether or not rent stabilization programs are effective or even desirable at all. The purpose of this literature review is to examine some of the various tradeoffs that exist when considering rent stabilization programs. 

Many scholars find rent stabilization programs to be very beneficial for tenants since they help protect against unjust rent increases and reduce the number of people displaced due to rent increases. Many scholars also point out that these policies help solve the problem of tenant displacement, thereby providing a more stable living situation. On the other hand, many researchers criticize these programs because they are said to discourage the development of new housing and reduce the amount of maintenance done on existing units. This review will examine scholarly articles on the effectiveness of rent stabilization programs in regards to their impact on rents, housing supply, property values, landlord behavior, and tenant displacement. The results of these studies will be used to highlight the various tradeoffs associated with rent stabilization.

Studying biostatistics will enable me to engage with these processes.

Specifically, I am interested in how biostatistics addresses problems with real-world implications, both for individuals and populations. Biostatistics plays an important role in the evaluation of treatment efficacy, risk factor identification, and health inequities. In all of these domains, the biostatistician’s role is to identify whether observed trends and associations represent true effects or merely random noise. I am motivated by this blend of mathematical analysis and tangible impact, and the fact that a biostatistician’s work can have direct implications for clinical practice and health policy is particularly appealing.

Biostatistics is an exciting field of study because it allows me to develop competencies in statistical modeling, study design, data analysis, and scientific communication. It would give me the opportunity to learn about handling messy data, biases, and ethical considerations, among others. Furthermore, the interdisciplinary aspect of biostatistics is one I find appealing. Biostatisticians frequently work with clinicians, epidemiologists, lab scientists, and policymakers. It is gratifying to know that through statistical analysis, we can not only identify what has happened but also suggest what should be done next. Graduate study in biostatistics will equip me with the training and resources to realize this goal and make an impact in biomedical and public health research.

How do I prepare for a 100-mile century? This is a 16-week training plan to take you from a novice rider to a cyclist ready to tackle a 100-mile century. Weeks 1-4: Establish your training foundation. Ride 3-4 times per week. The midweek ride should be 45-60 minutes at an easy/moderate pace. Your long ride for the weekend will be 25 miles in week 1, then add 5 miles each week until you reach 40 miles in week 4. Weeks 5-8: Add some intensity. Once a week, add some hills or intervals to your midweek ride to build leg strength. Midweek rides should still be at a moderate intensity. Long rides should be increased to 45 miles in week 5 and continue to add 5 miles each week until you reach 60 miles in week 8. Start experimenting with nutrition on long rides: aim for 30-60 grams of carbs and 1 bottle of water/electrolytes per hour. Weeks 9-12: Hit the peak. Continue with the same training as the previous block. Long rides should be 70 miles in week 10 and 80-85 miles in week 12. If you can do 85 miles, 100 miles should feel effortless with the rush of adrenaline, and drafting, on event day. Weeks 13-16: Taper and ride! Reduce your mileage throughout the block to allow your body to rest and rebuild. Your long ride should be 50 miles in week 14 and 30 miles in week 15. During the last week of the block, do 2 short, easy rides. Sleep well, hydrate, and get ready to ride your century.

### 10 Things To Know About Training For Your First Sprint Triathlon

Okay, so you want to do a sprint triathlon. That’s great! But if you’ve never done one before, you might be wondering how to train for your first one. Well, here are ten tips to help you cross that finish line feeling like a total winner.

1. **Create a training plan.** Find a beginner training plan and stick to it. It’ll be worth it in the long run.

2. **Do each discipline at least once.** Swimming, biking, running, they’re all required. Make sure you can do them all comfortably.

3. **Buy some gear.** You don’t need to go crazy, but buy yourself a good bike and goggles. Your future self will thank you.

4. **Practice your open water swimming.** If you’re not confident in your swimming skills, try practicing in a pool. There’s no reason to be embarrassed about it.

5. **Strength train twice a week.** This will prevent injuries and make your training more manageable. It’s a win-win situation.

6. **Practice your transitions.** Switching from sport to sport is harder than it sounds. Practice it a few times to make it easier.

7. **Rest when you need to.** Training hard is good, but so is resting. Take breaks when you need them.

8. **Wear your race outfit during training.** Try out your clothes, food, and equipment during training. It’s always better to know what works before race day.

9. **Find a group.** Join a local triathlon club or find some people to train with. It’ll be fun and helpful.

10. **It’s okay to be nervous.** You’re doing something difficult. Being nervous means you care about doing well. It’s perfectly normal.

Good luck! You’ll be glad you did it. Keep up with your training and you’ll feel great on race day.

When we experience extreme weather, it changes our understanding of what it means to own a home. It reminds us that our home is not just a private property, but a fragile part of a complex ecosystem. For many people, homeownership is the ultimate symbol of stability, freedom, and financial security. But extreme weather events like floods, wildfires, hurricanes, heat waves, and storms threaten that security. A house can become an unsafe investment if it's located in a high-risk area, if insurance becomes too expensive, or if power and water services are disrupted on a regular basis. Extreme weather changes how people think about buying and maintaining a home. People are beginning to think more carefully about the location and type of housing they want, taking into account factors like floodplain maps, wildfire risk, stormwater runoff, building materials, energy efficiency, and proximity to backup power sources. Homeowners are investing more in features like flood-proofing, fire-resistant roofs, backup generators, and better insulation. However, not everyone can afford these upgrades, and lower-income families can get trapped in dangerous areas, face rising insurance premiums, or lose their homes altogether. Extreme weather challenges the idea of homeownership as an individual endeavor. Instead, homeownership is a shared endeavor, dependent on decisions made by local governments, including how we zone land, build infrastructure, and respond to emergencies. We will need to decide who bears the cost of protecting homes and ensuring safe conditions for those who cannot easily move. Extreme weather might even force some people to abandon homeownership entirely and choose renting, living in a co-op, or relocating with government assistance. Ultimately, extreme weather forces us to rethink what it means to own a home. It forces us to consider a wider range of values, including resilience, environmental sustainability, affordability, and community. A home is still valuable, but its value now depends on much more than just its physical structure.

Tyler Chen used to love baseball. But after two seasons of year-round baseball on a top-tier travel team, including practices four times a week and tournaments every weekend, the 10-year-old right-hander decided he wanted no part of organized sports anymore.

“He was burnt out,” said his mom, Sarah Chen. “He didn’t want to do it anymore.”

Chen is not alone. Sports doctors and sports psychologists say they are seeing a significant increase in burnout among young athletes because of what is called sports specialization. Specialization is the early and intensive focus on a single sport at the expense of all others. The promise of athletic scholarships to big-name colleges and the growth of a $30-billion youth sports industry have led to a rise in year-round sports programs for children as young as 7. But specialists say the trend is causing injuries and creating an emotional burden that some kids can’t handle.

“We’re seeing more injuries that are overuse-related,” Dr. Elizabeth Murray, a pediatric sports medicine physician, said. “We’re seeing more and more cases of middle schoolers getting Tommy John surgery.” And even more concerning, specialists say, are kids who develop stress and anxiety disorders and depression when they don’t perform as well as they once did. “For many young athletes, it can feel like they’ve lost their identity if they can’t continue to perform,” Murray said.

Specialists say that the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommendations are clear: Kids should focus on one sport only after puberty, around age 15 or 16, and that the AAP recommends that children participate in several sports. This can help prevent overuse injuries, encourage lifelong healthy habits, and keep exercise fun. And despite the allure of scholarships and a $30-billion industry, a child doesn’t need to specialize to succeed. About 70 percent of kids who played organized sports quit by the time they’re 13, according to the National Alliance for Youth Sports.

With youth sports growing more like pro sports, those who oppose the rise of sports specialization are hoping to educate parents and coaches about the importance of giving kids downtime and encouraging them to play freely. For children like Tyler Chen, the consequences of too much focus have already set in. But for him, life is good again. He plays outside and rides bikes with his friends from the neighborhood, and is having fun.

There are privacy issues with facial recognition technology, but over-regulating it is bad for business and creates laws that are not effective in practice.

It’s argued that facial recognition can be used for mass surveillance and violates civil rights. But laws can’t stop people from making facial recognition technology. If the government regulates facial recognition too much in a democratic society, authoritarian governments and criminals are going to make it anyway.

Furthermore, too much regulation doesn’t take into account the good things that facial recognition does. Police use facial recognition to find suspects in crimes, missing children and human traffickers. Banks use it to prevent identity theft and verify user identities. Researchers use it to help understand genetic diseases. Strict regulation would prevent all those good uses along with the bad ones.

The real issue with regulation is that it isn’t flexible enough. Technologies change faster than law. Instead of trying to make laws that won’t keep up, governments should focus on accuracy, disclosure and accountability for users of facial recognition. Companies should disclose how facial recognition is being used, and victims should be able to get compensation if they are incorrectly identified by facial recognition software. But none of that requires banning the technology.

In addition, different governments regulate facial recognition differently, which creates complicated compliance requirements without improving privacy. A picture of me posted on a U.S. social media service can still be scanned for facial recognition anywhere in the world, no matter what U.S. laws say.

Instead of trying to ban facial recognition, lawmakers should provide specific examples of how facial recognition should or shouldn’t be used and invest in auditing to make sure those rules are followed. Regulations are most effective when they provide minimum standards that allow new products to be created. With facial recognition, a lighter touch will be more effective at protecting privacy than regulations that push facial recognition underground or abroad.

Unlimited vacation, also known as “discretionary time off” or “flexible leave”, has become a popular form of employee benefit offered by companies to help them retain and recruit workers. Unlike traditional paid time off (PTO), where employees have a predetermined amount of vacation time and must accumulate it over a period of time, unlimited vacation allows employees to take time off whenever necessary, with manager approval and within the context of business needs. Advocates of unlimited vacation argue that offering unlimited vacation time communicates organizational trust, encourages work-life balance, and meets modern expectations regarding employee flexibility and autonomy. In tight labor markets, these benefits could provide an edge in recruiting and retaining talent, especially among knowledge workers or those who prefer greater control over the timing and nature of their work.

Nevertheless, the association between unlimited vacation and retention is not so simple. While flexible leave may increase employee satisfaction by removing some of the restrictions on their ability to take time off for themselves, their families, or medical reasons, the lack of clarity inherent in an unlimited policy could lead to confusion among employees. Workers may be unsure of how much vacation time is appropriate, particularly in organizations with strong performance cultures or where understaffing limits the number of people who can be away from their jobs at any one time. Studies show that when there is ambiguity about work expectations, employees may choose to take less vacation time than they would otherwise, particularly if they are concerned about the impression they may make if they take more leave than other team members. The success of an unlimited vacation policy depends on a range of factors including organizational culture, management practices, workloads, employee confidence in voicing concerns, and whether managers use the policy themselves.

According to the research on turnover, salary and benefits alone rarely dictate whether an employee will stay with a company or leave. Factors like job satisfaction, perceived organizational support, fairness, burnout, career development, and supervisor-employee interactions all play a role in determining whether an individual remains employed by a given employer. As such, unlimited vacation is likely to be most successful when used in conjunction with other employee benefits, rather than as a singular employee perk. When combined with adequate staffing levels, clear usage policies, positive role modeling, and equal access to leave opportunities across different positions, unlimited vacation may help employees feel valued by their employer. This paper reviews the existing research on unlimited vacation and its impact on employee well-being, employee norms, perceived organizational support, and employee retention.

To prepare for a system-design interview, focus on developing a process for designing systems from vague requirements that can be repeated and refined in different contexts. Review the basic principles of scalability, availability, consistency, latency, partitioning, replication, caching, load balancing, queues, databases, and failure recovery, and learn when to use one over another. Know the difference between SQL and NoSQL, synchronous and asynchronous communication, and strong and eventual consistency, and be prepared to justify your choice. Practice designing common systems like a URL shortener, messaging system, social feed, file system, ride-sharing app, and video streaming service. For each, follow a consistent process: ask clarifying questions, estimate scale, design the API and data model, sketch the high-level architecture, identify bottlenecks and failure modes, and revisit trade-offs. Speak out loud while practicing and time yourself, as interviewers care just as much about your thought process as your final design. Don't dive into details too early, and avoid saying there's only one right answer. Study real-world system designs and read about how companies solve problems at scale. Prepare a framework, practice estimation, and get comfortable asking questions. In the interview, work with the interviewer, admit uncertainty, and adapt when new requirements or constraints emerge.

10 Tips for Introducing a Rescue Cat to an Apartment

Bringing a rescue cat home is a wonderful experience. But if you’re moving your new friend from the shelter to your apartment, there are a few things you should know. Here are 10 quick tips to help your new feline friend adjust.

**1. Give them their own space**
Keep the cat in a smaller area of the apartment initially. A bathroom or spare bedroom with a water bowl, litter box and food bowl is perfect. 

**2. Avoid loud noises**
Don’t invite guests over immediately after adopting your new friend. Your cat may get startled by loud noises or too many people. 

**3. Create hiding places**
Rescue cats don’t always like to feel exposed. Leave the carrier door open, or set up a cardboard box and line it with a blanket for your cat to hide in.

**4. Keep the litter box out of high traffic areas**
If you live in a two story loft, keep a litter box on each floor until your cat gets comfortable with the whole space. 

**5. Install screens on your balcony**
When you’re ready to let your cat outside, make sure your balcony is completely enclosed. Cats can climb up screens easily, so make sure your cat is safe before opening up the sliding glass door. 

**6. Keep feeding times consistent**
Keep your cat fed and hydrated at the same time each day. 

**7. Use synthetic pheromones**
There are pheromone products that mimic those found in nature, like Feliway. Plug one of these in your cat’s safe space and watch the effect it has. 

**8. Seal up tight spaces**
Don’t let your cat crawl under heavy furniture or behind appliances. Cover these areas with cardboard boxes, tape or other materials.

**9. Give them something to climb**
A tall cat tree or cat window perch gives your cat a place to retreat to and observe your apartment. 

**10. Let your cat make the decision**
Some cats will take to their new home in just a couple of hours, while others take a few weeks to get comfortable. Give them space and let them make the choice whether or not they want to cuddle with you.

One of the biggest advantages of POD has been the way it has revolutionized the economics of self-publishing. Prior to the advent of POD, self-publishing was prohibitively expensive and fraught with financial risk for most authors. Books were produced using an offset printing process, which required authors to order books in large quantities of hundreds or thousands at a time. Before even beginning the marketing process, authors had to invest thousands of dollars to print their books, while also paying for the storage of excess inventory. Many authors ended up with boxes of books they could not sell, and the risk of such a situation discouraged many writers from even attempting self-publishing.

The introduction of POD has completely overturned this model. With POD, books are printed one at a time when an order is received. Rather than investing upfront in hundreds of copies, an author can now wait until an order is placed and have the book printed for a specific customer. The cost of printing is then deducted from the revenue generated by the sale. This has turned self-publishing from a high-investment venture into a relatively low-risk venture for authors, and has enabled many authors to publish books on a very limited budget. Although the per-unit cost of a book printed via POD is higher than the cost of a book printed using offset printing, the elimination of upfront investment means that the overall cost of publishing a book is much lower with POD. Also, many POD services offer integration with online retailers, making it easy to get books into the hands of customers anywhere in the world without ever having to ship them. These improvements have led to an enormous increase in the number of self-published books being produced every year.

With the increase in suburban growth, communities are looking to expand public transportation. Housing growth, increased traffic, and longer commutes are increasing the need for better bus and rail services. Transit advocates emphasize the importance of investing in public transportation to maintain sustainable growth.

In growing suburbs, residents without cars, including seniors, students, and low-income individuals, are increasingly isolated from work, school, and medical services. Expanded service reduces traffic and enables denser development around stations and bus routes. But finding the money for expansion is a constant struggle.

Most suburban transit operators are funded with local taxes, state grants, and federal funds, which are not always consistent. Unlike major cities with established transit systems and dedicated revenue streams, many suburban communities are building routes and facilities from scratch. Some local officials are considering sales-tax increases, special assessment districts, and public-private partnerships to pay for expansion. Others are hoping to use federal transportation grants to buy electric buses, upgrade stops, or extend rail lines. Proponents claim that the investment will bring long-term benefits by attracting businesses and increasing property values along transit corridors.

However, skeptics argue that new transit systems will not draw sufficient ridership to justify their expense. They fear that costly projects could become a burden for taxpayers while failing to reduce automobile usage in low-density areas.

For suburban transit to succeed, it must offer frequent, affordable service and connect to other transit services. Zoning reform can also promote transit-oriented development, increasing the demand for transit service. As more people move into suburbs, the question of how to fund transit will remain a contentious issue. The outcome of this debate will shape whether suburban growth results in communities that rely on cars, or ones in which transit is an acceptable means of travel.

The idea that community libraries have no place in the digital age is a short-sighted one, one that underestimates their changing and important role. Information is more readily available than ever through digital resources, but in this new era, libraries are increasingly important community hubs. They help bridge the digital divide, drive intellectual development in their communities and do things technology simply can't.

Rather than simply holding physical books, today's libraries are an important point of access for people at a disadvantage in the digital world. Through free access to the internet, computers and digital skills, they help such people engage in an increasingly online world. Without them, many would be shut out of education, work and essential services.

Through workshops, book clubs, cultural events and more, libraries build community and offer space for intellectual exchange. In an often digitally isolated age, they represent a place for connection, learning and experience. They bring together trusted information, expert advice and a space for focused study. And they do this in contrast to often unverified and overwhelming information available online.

Community libraries are not of a bygone era. They are changing institutions, well suited to the digital age. They support digital inclusion in their communities, help build community and offer a trusted, curated space for knowledge and connection in addition to (and not in place of) the digital world. Above all, they need institutional support if there is to be an informed, socially connected society.

In recent years, social media, streaming services and e-commerce sites have radically changed the way consumers find, choose and consume products, content and information. Underlying this change is the recommendation algorithm, a computational tool that seeks to identify, from the many options available to a user, a small set of products, content or information likely to interest them. Over time, as algorithms have become more complex (incorporating, for example, collaborative, content and deep learning approaches), increasing attention has been paid in academic work across marketing, information systems, psychology and computer science to their impact on consumer decision-making.

Much of this earlier work focused on the effectiveness of recommendation systems, on, for example, performance of the algorithm and the accuracy of its predictions. But as more people encountered recommendations in their day-to-day lives, scholars started to ask what impact they might have psychologically and behaviorally. Do recommendation algorithms help consumers by cutting through information overload and search costs? Or do they constrain the choice architecture, reinforcing existing preferences, limiting choice and potentially creating "filter bubbles"? And how might, for example, trust in recommendations, their perceived personalization and the element of serendipity support purchase intentions and satisfaction?

Taken together, much of this work has raised questions about whether recommendation systems improve the quality of consumer choice, diversity in their consumption and their ability to make decisions. Some scholars argue they help consumers pick up options they would not otherwise have considered. Others warn that, through algorithmic curation, they risk undermining consumer judgment and encouraging similar consumption across large numbers of people. And there are concerns of manipulation, bias and lack of transparency in these systems. Taken together, these factors have made it difficult to assess the impact of recommendations on consumer agency.

In this paper, the review draws on previous academic work on the impact of recommendation algorithms on consumer choice. It considers theoretical perspectives, evidence and methods providing the foundation for that work. The purpose is to highlight areas of agreement and disagreement in the existing evidence, to point to gaps in the knowledge and to suggest possible future research on this increasingly important element of consumer decision-making.

# How to Request a Promotion After a Major Project Launches

### Timing Matters
Wait a couple of weeks after launching a project before you ask to meet with your manager. In that time, you can see what happened in the project and stakeholders will have time to think about its impact. If you ask for a meeting right away, it will appear that you're more opportunistic than strategic. Gather some tangible outcomes from the project: cost saving, revenue, user take-up or efficiency.

### Document Your Impact
Pinpoint your role in them. Note where you stepped up, mentored others, or solved key problems. This isn't self-promotion. It's evidence of your role. Point to something in the project that was outside your role. What did it bring out in you?

### Prepare a Clear Narrative
Link your development to what's required at the next level in your career. Show in specific ways that you were already operating at that level. Ask your manager for a meeting, rather than bringing it up out of nowhere. In your email, you could say something like: "I'd like to talk about my career development and my contributions. Do you have time this week?"

### Schedule Strategically
That shows professionalism. And it gives your manager time to think. Start by recognizing the opportunities you've had in the project. Then, non-defensively, outline your contributions. For example, "I drove cross-functional work on this project, which delivered on budget and on time." Then say: "Given my role here, I think I could move into [position]. What do you think?"

### During the Conversation
Your manager may agree, suggest next steps or point out weaknesses in your case. If he or she isn't sure, ask: "What would it take for me to move forward?" Write down his or her comments and draw up an action plan. If he or she says no, set up a check-in point for three months' time.

### Listen to Feedback
Over that period, keep adding value and act on feedback from your manager. If he or she says yes, put in writing what was discussed. A promotion request isn't about entitlement. It's about making a case that your contributions (beyond your original role) deserve greater recognition. Done well, such a request will support your career progression over time.

# 10 Tips for Choosing a Beginner-Friendly Telescope

Buying your first telescope can be be confusing. It doesn't have to be. Here are ten tips for people thinking of buying a telescope they'll enjoy using.

1. Disregard the "highest magnification" marketing.
Magnifications sound impressive, but more important than magnification is the quality of the optics. A sharp, stable image is more useful than one that's magnified but blurry.

2. Prioritize aperture.
Aperture is the size of a telescope's main lens or mirror. The larger the aperture, the more light it will gather and the more easily you could, for example, see the Moon, planets and faint objects in the sky.

3. Begin with a straightforward mount.
Most easily used by a beginner would be an alt-azimuth mount (one that swings up and down and left and right). More complicated mounts risk frustrating the set-up process.

4. Consider a tabletop Dobsonian.
Often good value, easy to point and stable, these little reflector telescopes could well suit an adult or a younger person.

5. Avoid department-store telescopes.
Often, inexpensive telescopes come with fancy packaging and a flimsy tripod. They rarely meet expectations. Better value for money would be a small, well-made telescope from a good astronomy retailer.

6. Account for portability.
Best of all, a telescope is only as good as the person using it. An overly complicated or heavy telescope may well sit unused.

7. Do not overlook binoculars.
A good pair of 7x50 or 10x50 binoculars would be a good starting point. They're easy to use and can open up the night sky in a very rewarding way.

8. Evaluate included accessories.
Good standard equipment for a telescope would be a finder scope, two eyepieces and a mount. At this stage you don't need a huge range of accessories.

9. Make use of astronomy applications.
Software such as SkySafari or Stellarium can help you find constellations, planets and stars. With it, your first night out with a telescope would be less daunting.

10. Maintain realistic expectations.
Planets won't look like those in NASA photos, but it's still a special experience to see, say, Jupiter's moons or the rings of Saturn through your telescope.

A good starting point would be to keep things simple, focus on enjoyment and spend a few nights getting to know the sky. Your first telescope doesn't need to be great. It just needs to encourage you to look up.

Self-checkout changes the nature of the relationship between the shopper and the store. It replaces human interaction with efficiency in the transaction. Traditionally, the grocery counter was a place for quick interactions, small talk with neighbors and contact with a brand through the people working there. With self-checkout, stores no longer see their customers as people to be served. Rather, they become participants in the labor process.

In this way, shoppers are at once more empowered and more alienated. For some, self-checkout is a faster, more private and more empowering way to leave the store. They may prefer to engage with the world through their screens and may well find small talk at the counter stressful.

But in the self-checkout lane, the shopper is under constant surveillance from indicator lights, weight sensors and cameras. Where once there might well have been mutual goodwill between shopper and store, now there is more likely mutual suspicion. If, for example, the scanner fails to read an item, an automated voice will stop the transaction. A monitor at the store will then have to step in. Suddenly the shopper is no longer a customer but a possible shoplifter.

In this way, self-checkout takes warmth out of the retail environment. By shifting labor to the customer, stores save money but risk losing loyalty to their brand. And when every interaction at the store is through some impersonal interface, the store becomes less of a fixture in the community and more like a warehouse. No longer is the relationship between shopper and store one of service. More often it would be one of utility. And in that sense, a human encounter becomes a series of individual beeps.

# The Rise of Newsletter Writers as Trusted News Sources

In an age of declining trust in traditional media, independent writers of newsletters have become powerful commentators in public life. Through analysis, insight and perspective on everything from technology to politics, these writers have built loyal audiences.

In part, this reflects a shift in how people engage with information. Rather than sifting through ads and algorithmically-curated content on a news site, a newsletter brings content straight into a reader's inbox. And the reader chooses to subscribe. In that sense, trust supports the relationship between writer and reader, rather than algorithmic suggestion.

"Readers want expertise they can grasp," says media analyst Sarah Chen. "Often mainstream media lacks personality and context, but newsletter writers provide that."

Over time, some of these writers have built up considerable influence. Through platforms such as Substack, they can now sell content directly to readers rather than, for example, relying on advertising or institutional support. And in many areas -- politics, economics, science and culture -- they reach audiences comparable to those of traditional publications.

Much of their success stems from a deep focus on a particular topic. Over time many of these writers have developed expertise in their area.

Often they bring a consistent voice and perspective to their work. That lets their readers know where they stand, rather than having to guess at any underlying bias in their writing. And many build up a relationship with their readers through feedback mechanisms in their newsletters.

But there are challenges in this boom in newsletters. There is so much information now that it is difficult for readers to know what's good. And in the absence of editorial input, some writers have spread misinformation.

And readers rightly question accountability and transparency in this increasingly fragmented media environment. Many of journalism's more experienced practitioners now run their own newsletters alongside their institutional roles. In this sense, they are adding to, rather than replacing, traditional media.

Increasingly, readers turn to newsletter writers for analysis they trust, in a form that suits them. In that sense, they are changing the way modern media is consumed.

Hybrid learning is not the death of the university lecture, but rather its evolution. For centuries, lectures have allowed experts to present difficult ideas, shape knowledge and intellectually challenge their students. In turn, students have often found in lectures an opportunity to ask deeper questions. But in today's world, the lecture format -- in which students sit in a lecture hall at a particular time to listen to an expert -- doesn't meet students' needs. In the right circumstances, hybrid learning could build on the strengths of the lecture, while overcoming its limitations.

In a hybrid model, students would combine online elements (discussion boards, digital assessments, recorded lectures and virtual office hours) with face-to-face teaching. In this way, students could move at their own pace through difficult material, build on their studies when they are ill, have work commitments or need to commute. And they could more easily access a course if they live far from campus or have a disability.

Some argue that through online elements, a sense of community at university is lost. This concern is valid. Through debate, discussion, informal interaction with peers and faculty, as well as through course content, students learn at university. But that doesn't mean such interaction has to disappear in a hybrid model. Rather, it could become more focused. Rather than lecturers repeating material available online, in class they could use time for case work, problem-solving, lab work, discussion of difficult ideas and formative feedback.

In future, then, the lecture would more often be an intellectual event between professor and student than a lecture by the professor. More than ever, professors will be essential in a lecture. Not just to present information, but to challenge assumptions, explain difficult ideas and provoke discussion. Technology could support this role, but it could not replace it.

Best of all, hybrid learning should be supported by thought about pedagogy, not used as a cheaper alternative to teaching. To make hybrid learning work well, universities could support faculty in using it, ensure all students had access to technology, and build more interactive courses. If they choose to, through hybrid learning, higher education could become more engaging, inclusive and flexible. And in an increasingly changing academic world, the lecture could well retain its value.

Rent stabilization programs are intended to address housing affordability and prevent tenant displacement. They sit at the heart of a highly contested area of urban policy with often conflicting economic and social trade-offs. Underlying the case for such interventions is the view that in an unregulated housing market, low-income households may well be denied affordable housing. And where this happens, we could see rent spikes and declining security for tenants. But in practice, rent stabilization raises difficult questions for policymakers, economists and housing advocates about its impact and value. In this literature review, we consider the range of trade-offs involved in rent stabilization programs. We look at what they may achieve for tenants and at unintended consequences of their introduction.

Much of the literature argues that through the restraint of rent increases, rent stabilization supports tenant security, helps avoid unjustified rent increases in rapidly gentrifying neighborhoods and more fairly allocates housing in the city. But another powerful argument is that rent stabilization distorts the market, reduces incentives for maintenance and development of housing and could in the longer term reduce housing supply and quality. In this review, we consider both arguments. Drawing on evidence of the impact of rent stabilization on property values, housing supply, rental prices, landlord behavior and tenant welfare, we seek to illuminate the economic and social trade-offs inherent in such programs. In particular, we aim to pick up some of the debate in policy and academic discussions about the value of rent stabilization.

A 100-mile century is a demanding event. To succeed, a progressive training plan over 16 weeks is required. In this period the training builds cardiovascular endurance, muscular stamina and nutrition.

### Weeks 1–4: Building the Base
Three or four rides a week, at a similar pace each time, is the focus here. In the week, do a 45- to 60-minute ride at a moderate pace. And at the weekend, do the key long ride in the training plan. Start at 25 miles in week 1, add 5 miles each week and by week 4 the distance will be 40 miles.

### Weeks 5–8: Increasing Volume and Intensity
Once a week, add hill work or intervals to build strength in the legs. Keep the mid-week rides active but doable. Over the weekend, the long ride will build from 45 miles in week 5 to 60 miles in week 8. Starting in these long rides, begin experimenting with nutrition on the bike. Aim for one bottle of water or electrolytes and 30-60g of carbs each hour.

### Weeks 9–12: Peak Mileage
In this phase of training the physical challenge of the event is building up. Each week, add a little more distance in the mid-week rides. And the long ride will peak. Aim for 70 miles in week 10 and 80-85 miles in week 12. Assuming in training 85 miles is possible, on event day the last 15 miles can be pushed through using drafting and adrenaline.

### Weeks 13–16: Tapering and Event Day
Over the following weeks, distance should come down to let the muscles adapt. In week 14, cut the long ride back to 50 miles. In week 15, to 30. In week 16, do two easy, short spins to keep the legs ready. Hydrate well in the week, get plenty of sleep and go into the start line feeling ready and strong.

# 10 Tips for Training for Your First Sprint Triathlon

You've decided to do a sprint triathlon. That's no small ask. Don't worry if you're new to triathlon. Here are a few tips to help you feel up to the challenge of crossing that finish line.

1. Start with a plan.
Pick a 12-week training plan for a beginner and stick with it. You'll be rewarded for your consistency.

2. Practice all three disciplines.
Each of the three disciplines -- swimming, cycling and running -- needs attention. To do well in the race, you'll need some competence in all three.

3. Invest in the basics.
You don't need expensive equipment, but a good pair of swim goggles, a decent bike and some swim sessions in the pool would all add up to good value over the course of your training.

4. Build your swimming confidence.
If you're intimidated by open water, it would be perfectly reasonable to start with sessions in the pool.

5. Do not skip strength training.
Twice a week, add some strength work to your routine. It will improve your performance in all three disciplines and cut down on injury risk.

6. Nail your transitions.
Through training, practice moving from one discipline to another. This is one of the trickiest parts of the race, but also one of the easiest to improve.

7. Listen to your body.
In training, you need intensity, but you also need recovery. That doesn't mean you haven't committed to your training. Physiologically, you need rest days.

8. Test everything beforehand.
In training, try out your race outfit, nutrition plan and equipment. This isn't the time on race day to experiment with anything.

9. Find your people.
A local triathlon club or training partners would add motivation and support to your training that would be hard to get on your own.

10. Embrace the nerves.
This is a challenging event for you. It's natural to feel anxious about it. And that anxiety would probably be there even if you hadn't signed up. It's a sign you care about the result.

Trust your training, stay consistent with it and remember what drew you to sign up in the first place.

In a short space of time, you'll join a thriving community of triathletes.

Now go and give it a go.

Extreme weather is showing that a house is both a private asset and part of an environmental system. For many years, people have seen homeownership as a source of security, independence and financial stability. But in the face of floods, wildfires, hurricanes, heat, severe storms and other extreme weather, that promise is undermined. A house in a risky location, with inadequate insurance or failing infrastructure, can quickly lose value.

In response, people are increasingly thinking about square footage, school districts, flood maps, wildfire risk, drainage, energy efficiency and building materials when they consider where to live. And they are increasingly thinking about home improvements. Fire-resistant roofs, storm shutters, insulation, cooling systems, rain gardens and backup batteries, for example, once seemed like indulgences in many areas. Now they may be essential. But not everyone can retrofit a home. And sometimes even moving away isn't an option for low-income families. They may face higher insurance costs, lose a home or remain in a risky location.

In this way, extreme weather undercuts the idea that homeownership is an individual success. Whether people can safely live in a home depends in part on decisions about zoning, infrastructure, climate policy and emergency planning in a community. And communities need to ask: Who will pay for protection? And how do they help people in a home who can't easily move? In some places, frequent disaster may make government-supported relocation, cooperative housing, renting or other forms of ownership more sensible than traditional homeownership.

In short, extreme weather is forcing people to think of homeownership less as ownership of a fixed refuge and more as risk management. And it's pushing people to think of value in a home in more dimensions: environmental responsibility, affordability, safety and resilience. A home is still valuable. But increasingly its safety will depend on more than what's in it.

# CHICAGO

Ten-year-old Tyler Chen used to love playing baseball. But after two years of playing on a top-level travel team, four nights of practice a week and weekend trips, he decided he didn't want sports anymore.

"He just got tired of it," says his mother, Sarah Chen. "He lost his joy in it."

Increasingly, this is what's happening with kids. Sports psychologists and pediatricians warn of a growing problem of burnout in children at an early age through what's called sports specialization. That's when a child starts intensively training in one sport and drops others at a young age.

Seeing a chance of scholarships in college and drawn by the $30 billion a year youth sports industry, more parents are putting their kids into year-round sports as young as age 7. But according to experts, in many cases this focus backfires.

"We're seeing more overuse injuries in middle schoolers, for example Tommy John shoulder surgery, which used to only happen in pro athletes," says Dr. Elizabeth Murray, a pediatric sports medicine specialist. But more troubling to her is the emotional impact on kids. "Many of them are feeling chronic stress, anxiety and depression," she says. "They've put so much of their identity into their sport. And when they struggle or get injured, they feel like their identity is threatened."

The AAP recommends kids not specialize in one sport until they reach puberty, at least by age 15 or 16. Through multi-sport participation, the AAP says kids develop better athleticism, are less likely to get injured and are more likely to want to be active.

Today, 70 percent of kids drop out of organized sports by age 13, according to the National Alliance for Youth Sports.

More and more, youth sports is becoming professional. And many advocates would encourage more unstructured play for kids and more rest. In time, that message sunk in for Tyler. Now he spends his afternoons biking with his friends in the neighborhood. And slowly, he's started to rediscover the joy of physical activity.

# The Limits of Facial Recognition Regulation

Facial recognition technology is rightly seen as a privacy concern. But overly strict regulation risks stifling innovation and ends up with a useless regulatory framework.

Often we hear that facial recognition threatens civil liberties and facilitates mass surveillance. That argument misses the point that, even under regulation, determined parties could well develop or use facial recognition. Criminal gangs and authoritarian regimes will use such technology, no matter what the law says. By restricting facial recognition in our own society, we risk letting such technology develop elsewhere.

And restrictive regulation would rule out many useful applications of facial recognition. Banks use it for authentication and fraud detection. Law enforcement uses it to find missing children, prevent human trafficking and identify suspects in serious crime. And medical researchers use it in their work on genetic disease. By restricting facial recognition, we would be cutting off both good and bad uses.

A problem with regulation is that technology moves on much faster than legislation. And in many cases, regulation will quickly become outdated. Instead of setting rules that quickly become out of date, we could, for example, set transparency obligations, accuracy requirements and accountability for use of the technology as it develops.

Where a company uses facial recognition, it should inform its customers. And where it fails or is misused, they should have a remedy. That could be achieved without any ban on facial recognition.

In many jurisdictions regulations on facial recognition are very different. They add compliance burden but little privacy. A photo on a social media platform in the U.S. could well be subject to facial recognition analysis in other parts of the world.

Rather than trying to ban use of facial recognition, policymakers could set guidelines for its use in different situations. And they could build in mechanisms to audit its use. Best practice in regulation is to set minimum standards and let innovation thrive. And in the case of facial recognition, more permissive regulation would better protect privacy than one that pushed development into other jurisdictions or underground.

Increasingly, organizations are offering "unlimited vacation," often called "discretionary time off" or "flexible leave," as part of their package to employees. In many organizations, paid time off is a fixed entitlement, usually requiring employees to build up leave over time. With an unlimited vacation policy, however, in principle an employee could take time off from work at any point, depending on the needs of their role and their manager. Supporters of such policies see them as a sign of trust in employees, a way of supporting work-life balance and a better fit with employees' desire for autonomy and flexibility. In a competitive labor market, employees may well value this kind of policy, especially if they are knowledge workers or people who care about when and how they work.

But it's not clear that an unlimited vacation policy will necessarily improve retention. On the one hand, flexible leave could increase satisfaction for employees, freeing them up to meet their health, family and personal needs. On the other hand, under such a policy, they might not know how much leave would be appropriate in any given situation. Studies of workplace norms show that in the absence of clear expectations, employees tend to take less leave than they could under a formal entitlement. And they may well worry they would seem less committed than their colleagues. In practice, then, the impact of an unlimited vacation policy would depend on the culture of the organization, its workload, psychological safety for employees, and whether leaders were taking time off themselves.

Other work on retention shows that rarely, if ever, do compensation and benefits drive an employee's decision to stay with a company. Rather, employees consider, for example, career opportunities, fairness, burnout, their relationship with their manager and their satisfaction in their role. Unlimited vacation could well add value to a broader retention strategy, but probably wouldn't work on its own. With appropriate staffing, clear guidance on its use, supportive leadership and availability across roles, flexible leave could help employees feel their well-being was more valued by their organization. In this literature review, the author considers theoretical and empirical evidence on unlimited vacation policies. The review focuses on the impact of such policies on voluntary turnover intentions, perceived organizational support, workplace norms and well-being of employees.

Through this, I realized that when we lose an ecosystem, it is usually not just a particular habitat or species that is lost. More often, it is a whole network of ecological relationships supporting life in that system, and beyond. That realization sparked in me a curiosity about what sustains integrity in ecosystems and what human actions risk undermining it.

Over the years, this curiosity grew into an interest in habitat fragmentation, loss of biodiversity and the impacts of climate change. In that spirit, I have over the years got involved in citizen science projects to track populations of local species, worked with local environmental groups, and read widely in the literature on sustainable land management and restoration ecology. Through these experiences, I increasingly realized that in many ways, conservation is as much about sustaining fundamental ecological processes for human society as it is about conserving nature itself.

Most of all, what attracts me to the field of conservation ecology is that it brings together ecological theory, field work and quantitative analysis. To do so, I need to build up my knowledge of conservation ecology.

To do well in a system-design interview, more is needed than knowledge of architectures. Instead, a process is required for turning vague requirements into scalable, practical designs.

Start by getting up to speed with concepts such as scalability, availability, consistency, latency, partitioning, replication, caching, load balancing, queues, databases and failure recovery. More important than definitions of these concepts is understanding the trade-offs between them. For example, it should be possible to explain when NoSQL would be a better fit than SQL, when asynchronous would be better than synchronous, and when eventual consistency would be better than strong consistency.

Take a few typical design problems (e.g. social feeds, ride sharing, video, file storage, messaging and URL shortening) and work through them using the following approach:

1. Think through the requirements. What are the key data, users, traffic, latency, availability needs?
2. Think about capacity. Roughly how much storage, bandwidth, requests per second and growth would be needed? Be up front about assumptions here.
3. Think about the data model and API. They should reflect the main use cases.
4. Think about the architecture. How would services, databases, caches, queues, external systems and clients fit together?
5. Think about potential bottlenecks and failure points. How would the design handle retries, timeouts, backpressure, replication, monitoring and disaster recovery?
6. Think about trade-offs. Why would this design meet the requirements? And, at scale, what would need to change?

In practice, try to verbalize this process and use a timer. As much as technical knowledge, in an interview the focus will be on decision-making and communication. Don't get into implementation detail until a design is established. And don't argue that one approach is right for all situations.

Look at case studies of systems built by other engineers. And think about the architecture of systems already known. Before the interview, think of a framework for approaching design questions, practice doing capacity calculations and get comfortable asking clarifying questions.

In the interview, engage with the question, recognize when something is unknown, and let the design evolve as more constraints are introduced.

# 10 Tips for Introducing a Rescue Cat to a New Apartment

Taking a rescue cat home is one of the most satisfying things a new pet owner can do. But for many, moving from life in a shelter to life in an apartment can be very disorienting. Below are ten tips to help ensure a low-stress period of adjustment.

## 1. Start with a "safe zone"
Don't let the cat explore the whole apartment straight away. Instead, start with a small, quiet room (bedroom, bathroom) for the cat, complete with food, water and a litter box.

## 2. Keep it quiet
Avoid social events in the early days. In the first few days, the less noise the cat hears, the less likely it is to become frightened or stressed.

## 3. Provide hiding spots
When uncertain, cats tend to want to hide. A cardboard box covered with a soft blanket in the room or an open carrier would meet this need.

## 4. Keep the litter box accessible
Put the litter box somewhere quiet and out of the way. In a loft, you may well need a litter box on each floor at this stage.

## 5. Cat-proof your balcony
Cats can do well in an apartment with a balcony. But first, you need to make sure the balcony is enclosed with cat-safe netting, before letting the cat out.

## 6. Stick to a routine
It's a good idea to feed the cat at the same time every day. In rescue animals, regularity in their day seems to build a sense of security.

## 7. Use pheromones
Consider using a pheromone diffuser (e.g. Feliway) in the room where the cat is spending its time. It emits a chemical similar to ones produced naturally by cats. It works very well.

## 8. Block tight spaces
Check that there isn't a gap behind, say, a washing machine or under heavy furniture. The cat could get stuck there.

## 9. Go vertical
Apartments tend to have limited floor space. Wherever possible, use vertical space. A window perch or tall cat tree would let the cat look out over its new surroundings from a safe distance.

## 10. Let them set the pace
Every cat adjusts at a different pace. Some will settle in within hours of moving home. Others will take weeks. Don't push for physical contact. Let the cat decide when it's ready to approach you. Over time, with space, the cat will feel at home in its new surroundings.

Print-on-demand (POD) has upended the economics of self-publishing, removing the main obstacle for independent authors entering the market: up-front money. In the past, self-publishing meant commissioning hundreds or thousands of copies of a book. The author would then have to spend thousands of dollars before any sales could occur. That model put considerable financial risk on the author, forced him or her to hold inventory, and often left large amounts of unsold books.

With POD, books are printed on demand, copy by copy, in response to customer orders. Publishing thereby moved from an inventory business to an on-demand service. And what had been a high fixed-cost process became a variable-cost one. No longer would authors need to guess at demand for their book or take on production costs. Only after a sale would a book be printed, and costs would be taken out of the sale.

Through this, publishing has become accessible to writers with very limited resources. And calculations of profit on a book changed. Printing costs per book are higher under POD than under offset printing. Margins on each book would therefore be smaller. But in their place we now have no up-front investment and no inventory. And more importantly, the book could easily be sold on an online retail platform, anywhere in the world, with no need for warehousing.

Over time, we have seen far more self-published books. And where once the question would have been "can I afford to publish this book?", now it tends to be "will someone buy it?" In that sense, creative and entrepreneurial risk in publishing has become much lower.

With increasing population in the suburbs, local governments are being pushed to bring public transit to areas beyond the traditional city center. Congested roads, longer commutes and new housing developments have led many people in these auto-oriented communities to demand more reliable bus and rail service.

Transit supporters say investment in transit is needed if growth is to be sustainable. In many fast-growing suburbs, without transportation options, students, seniors, low-income workers and others may find themselves cut off from health care, schools, work and other important activities. And better transit could relieve traffic, encourage development along bus routes and at train stations and improve quality of life.

But often there isn't enough money to fund transit in the suburbs. Typically, transit agencies in suburbs draw on federal, state and local funding. Each of these can vary. And many suburbs are building transit facilities and routes from scratch.

Some local leaders have floated special assessment districts, sales tax increases and public-private partnerships to underwrite transit expansion. Others are seeking federal grants for rail extensions, better bus stops and electric buses. They point to potential long-term economic value of capital investment in transit, in the form of more property value and businesses along transit corridors.

Others doubt that new transit would attract enough riders to justify its cost. And they worry that in many low-density suburbs, large projects could add to taxes without reducing people's reliance on the car.

Transportation planners argue that more than just new routes, suburban transit needs to be frequent, affordable and linked to other transit. And with appropriate zoning and land use policies, residential and commercial development could well follow transit corridors. That, in turn, could support more riders.

Increasingly, as the suburbs take on more of the population, arguments will arise about how to fund transit there. And the decisions taken now will shape whether, in expanding suburbs, the result is more car-dependent communities or communities in which public transit could play a useful role in people's lives.

The view that community libraries are obsolete in the digital era is short-sighted and ignores their evolving and essential roles. Although digital resources provide unprecedented access to information, libraries are becoming vital centers for overcoming the digital divide and promoting intellectual development that cannot be achieved with technology alone.

Rather than serving solely as repositories for print materials, modern libraries provide essential access to the digitally disadvantaged. They offer free access to the Internet, to computer technology and to important training in digital literacy, and therefore facilitate equal participation in an increasingly technological world. Without libraries, millions of individuals would be denied access to essential health care, employment opportunities and educational resources.

Plus, libraries promote a sense of community and provide essential physical facilities that cannot be achieved with digital technology. They sponsor workshops, book discussion groups and cultural activities that stimulate interaction and intellectual development. In a world often characterized by digital isolation, they provide a physical basis for contact, learning and experience of which the Internet is incapable. They provide access to reliable information, to expert guidance and to conditions that support concentrated learning in contrast to the overwhelming and largely unverified information available on-line.

For that reason, community libraries are not obsolete; they represent dynamic institutions responding to the requirements of the digital age. They are critical components of efforts to achieve digital inclusion, to develop a sense of community and to provide a basis for access to reliable information and to experience of learning that complements rather than competes with the technological environment. Continued support for these activities is essential to the development of an informed and well-integrated society.

The explosive growth of e-commerce portals, streaming services and social networking sites has revolutionized the ways consumers discover and select products, information and services. Central to this transformation is the recommendation algorithm, a computational tool that predicts consumer preferences and narrows the overwhelming variety of available options to a manageable, personalized subset. With increasing sophistication based on collaborative filtering, content-based filtering and methods of machine learning, these algorithms now exert substantial influence on consumer decision processes and have attracted considerable attention from researchers in marketing, information systems, psychology and computer science.

Initial work in this area concentrated primarily on the technical performance of recommendation systems and on measures of accuracy and algorithmic efficiency. However, as these systems became more deeply integrated into everyday consumer experience, investigators extended their analyses to include broader behavioral and psychological effects. Questions arose regarding whether recommendation algorithms truly increase consumer welfare by reducing costs of search and information overload, or instead restrict the architecture of choice to the extent of limiting consumer autonomy, reinforcing pre-existing preferences and generating filter bubbles. Finally, the research examines the ways in which algorithmic recommendations modify perceived levels of trust, personalization and serendipity to influence consumer intentions and satisfaction.

Although the volume of published work continues to grow, major controversies remain concerning the overall effects of these systems on quality of consumer choice, diversity of consumption experiences and capacity for long-term decision making. Some investigators believe that these algorithms enhance consumer choice by providing access to options that would otherwise escape notice, whereas others contend that excessive reliance on algorithmic modes of information selection impairs capacity for independent judgment and promotes uniformity of patterns of consumption. Also, concerns about the degree of transparency, potential for manipulation and extent of algorithmic bias further impair our understanding of the ways in which these systems influence consumer autonomy.

This review integrates and summarizes the major results of previous work on the effects of recommendation algorithms on consumer behavior. The intent is to clarify points of agreement and disagreement, identify major gaps in knowledge and suggest directions for future research on this rapidly expanding area of consumer behavior.

However, exposure to George Lakoff's work on conceptual metaphor completely transformed my perspective, and led me to appreciate the extent to which our bodily experiences guide the construction of abstract thought. Examining how we project the physical world onto cognitive representations (e.g., by representing time as a spatial dimension) confirmed that language ultimately provides the most complete window into human cognition.

My goal is to pursue graduate training in cognitive linguistics to investigate the interface between language, mind and experience. In particular, I am especially interested in the extent to which mechanisms of conceptual integration and frame semantics account for our capacity for creative and ideological thought. In an age of rapid developments in artificial intelligence, it is more important than ever to understand uniquely human aspects of cognitive processing. Although large language models can replicate statistical properties of syntactic structure, they lack the experiential basis that underlies human representations of meaning. My research will focus on the processes by which representations of conceptual structure emerge from sensory-motor experience, and therefore distinguish human modes of semantic comprehension from mechanisms of machine learning.

# How to Ask for a Promotion After a Big Project Ships

### Timing Matters
Wait 2 to 4 weeks after project initiation to request a meeting. This allows time to evaluate results and provides distance for objective assessment of impact. Avoid immediate requests, which will appear opportunistic rather than strategic.

### Document Your Impact
Obtain concrete measures of revenue generated, costs avoided, degree of user acceptance or improvements in efficiency. Quantify your contributions fully. Describe episodes of leadership, provision of mentoring and resolution of critical problems.

### Prepare a Clear Narrative
This constitutes documentation of performance, not bragging. Explain the extent to which your responsibilities and capabilities were expanded by the project. Relate this experience to requirements for the next level of professional responsibility.

### Schedule Strategically
Demonstrate that you have achieved a level of performance appropriate for that higher level. Request a formal meeting with your manager, not an ambush. Communicate directly: "I would like to discuss my record of career development and contributions to the project.

### During the Conversation
Do you have time for a 30-minute discussion this week?" This conveys a professional image and provides time for preparation. Express appreciation for opportunities received and describe achievements without defensive attitudes. Provide details of "The project was completed on time and within budget, for which I coordinated activities among all functional areas." Ask explicitly: "Based on my performance, am I ready for promotion to [position]?" Your manager may accept this evaluation, outline plans for the next level of responsibility or identify deficiencies requiring correction.

### Listen to Feedback
If the response is equivocal, ask what additional experience or development is required. Prepare a written record of all discussions and develop an action plan for continued professional development. If the final determination is that promotion is not appropriate at this time, schedule a 90-day follow-up meeting.

### Follow Up
Continue to demonstrate the value of your work and respond to the requirements for further development. Finally, remember that requests for promotion represent an effort to obtain fair recognition for increases in responsibility and performance. When done professionally, these efforts reinforce your record of career development.

# 10 Tips for choosing a beginner-friendly telescope

Buying your first telescope may seem overwhelming, but it doesn't have to be. Here are 10 simple tips to help you select a telescope you will actually enjoy using.

1. Skip the “highest magnification” hype.
Large magnification numbers sound impressive, but image quality is far more important. A clear, steady view is always better than a fuzzy close-up.

2. Look at aperture first.
Aperture (the diameter of the telescope's primary lens or mirror) determines how much light the telescope can gather and therefore how easily you will see the Moon, planets and faint objects. A sturdy alt-azimuth mount (which moves up/down and left/right) is easiest for beginners and avoids the frustration of complicated setup procedures.

3. Start with a simple mount.
These inexpensive, stable telescopes are excellent choices for children and adults alike. Cheap telescopes with shaky tripod mounts and flashy packaging are generally disappointing.

4. Consider a tabletop Dobsonian.
Instead, it is better to purchase a smaller, well-built telescope from a reputable dealer. The best telescope is one that you will actually use.

5. Avoid department-store telescopes.
If it is too heavy or complicated for outdoor use, it will ultimately sit unused in a closet. Initial experience with astronomy is greatly enhanced by use of a good pair of 7x50 or 10x50 binoculars.

6. Think about portability.
They are easy to use and provide a highly enjoyable experience of star gazing. Essential accessories include two eyepieces, a finder telescope and a sturdy mounting system.

7. Don’t forget binoculars.
You do not need an extensive array of accessories at this time. Computer programs such as Stellarium or SkySafari will greatly assist you in identifying stars, planets and constellations and will make your first nights outdoors considerably less stressful.

8. Check what accessories are included.
Planetary images will not resemble photographs taken by NASA, but observations of Saturn's rings or of the moons of Jupiter will be totally exciting. Begin with simple equipment, enjoy the experience of learning to observe the sky, and ultimately develop a lifelong appreciation of astronomy.

9. Use astronomy apps.
Your first telescope need not be perfect to provide you with many hours of enjoyable outdoor experience.

10. Set realistic expectations.

Start simple, keep it fun, and spend a few nights learning the sky. Your first telescope doesn’t need to be perfect—it just needs to get you outside looking up.
